docs.text: Build and run ¶ Three builds come out of one tree, and each of them is a check of the portability as much as a product: Build What it produces Commands Directory host the unit tests and the simulator, as a Linux process make build , make test , make sim , make smoke build-host/ , build-asan/ , build-tsan/ x86-64 a bare-metal kernel and its loader, for QEMU make x86-build , make x86-run , make x86-smoke build-x86/ ESP32 the firmware of the board, through ESP-IDF v5.3 make idf-build , make idf-flash , make bundle build/ The null port ( ports/port_null ) has no build of its own: it is linked into the host build as microos_null_probe , and the link is the check. Dependencies ¶ Package Needed by Arch / CachyOS Debian / Ubuntu cmake , ninja every build cmake ninja cmake ninja-build gcc the host and x86 builds gcc gcc python3 the tools, the checks, ESP-IDF python python3 qemu-system-x86_64 running the x86-64 machine qemu-system-x86 qemu-system-x86 GTK backend of QEMU the window of make x86-run qemu-ui-gtk qemu-system-gui clang-format make format , the format check clang-format clang-format valgrind the cloud run of the tests, optional valgrind valgrind pyserial tools/console.py , tools/stream_console.py python3 -m pip install pyserial the same The packages of the last two columns are installed with sudo pacman -S --needed ... or sudo apt install ... . ESP-IDF is needed only for the board; it brings its own toolchain and Python environment. commands.md is the reference for the packages and for the variables that override the defaults. The host build ¶ make build # cmake -B build-host -S . -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug make test # build, then ctest: the unit tests and the null probe make test-asan # the same tests with the address and UB sanitizers make test-tsan # the same tests under the race detector make sim # build, then run build-host/ports/port_host/microos_sim make smoke # boot the simulator and check what it says The same by hand: cmake -B build-host -S . -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE = Debug cmake --build build-host ctest --test-dir build-host --output-on-failure build-host/ports/port_host/microos_sim The simulator is the whole system on a volume in a file: MicroFS, /proc , /dev , the configuration of /etc , the init scripts and the shell. The environment shapes it: Variable Meaning Default MICROOS_VOLUME the file of the MicroFS volume /tmp/microos-sim.img MICROOS_KV_DIR the directory of the key-value store /tmp/microos-kv MICROOS_SCREEN draw the console into this file instead of nowhere unset MICROOS_INPUT a script of button events for input unset make sim is interactive; make smoke ( tools/sim_smoke.py ) drives it with a list of commands and checks the transcript. make clean removes build-host/ and build-asan/ only: build-tsan/ and build/ stay. The x86-64 build ¶ make x86-build # the loader, the kernel and the programs, into build-x86/ make x86-all # the complete machine: network, disk and run.sh make x86-all-run # boot it in a window (x86-all-run-serial: a terminal) make x86-disk # build-x86/programs.img: /bin and /etc of MicroFS make x86-run # a QEMU window: VGA text and the PS/2 keyboard make x86-run-serial # the same machine in a terminal (-nographic) make x86-smoke # boot and check the transcript, no window make x86-vga-smoke # check the screen and the keyboard without a display make x86-run-disk # the window with a disk of its own, kept between runs make x86-run-disk-serial # the same disk in a terminal make x86-disk-smoke # two boots on one image: a file survives both The build is a CMake project of its own ( ports/port_x86_64 ), because the kernel there has no libc under it. The machine boots from three files: build-x86/loader32.elf (a multiboot loader that QEMU takes with -kernel ), build-x86/microos64.bin (the flat kernel image) and build-x86/programs.img (the disk). The programs of /bin are built first ( hello.mox , crash.mox , fork.mox , badptr.mox , ...) and written into a MicroFS volume of the disk by tools/mkfs_mfs.c ; the kernel carries no copy of a program, and the boot mounts the volume and reads /bin/hello with execve . make x86-all is the machine a person can start without knowing which of the builds it is made of: build-x86-all/ holds loader32.elf , microos64.bin , x86-all.img (the disk with /bin and /etc ) and a run.sh that boots the three with a virtio-net card on the user network of QEMU (port 8080 forwarded). X86_SERIAL=1 ./build-x86-all/run.sh gives the serial console and no window. The target is not make bundle ; the release artifact is still the one of tools/bundle.sh . The display backend is a package of its own in some distributions: the target asks QEMU for its list of backends first and prints the command to run when the one asked for is missing. make x86-run X86_DISPLAY=sdl picks SDL, and make x86-run-serial is the machine for a box without a display server at all. The disk is a raw image of 8 MB, made by make x86-disk ( tools/mkfs_mfs.c , which links components/mfs ) and kept in build-x86/programs.img ; make x86-run-disk copies it once to build-x86/disk.img and keeps that copy between runs. Both are generated, not committed; make clean does not remove build-x86/ , so rm -rf build-x86 is the way to start over. The details are in the port's README, docs/ports/x86_64/README.md . The ESP32 build ¶ make idf-build finds ESP-IDF on its own, in this order: $IDF_PATH , a checkout beside the repository ( ../esp-idf ), then ~/esp/esp-idf . Point it elsewhere with IDF_EXPORT=/path/to/export.sh ; there is no need to source export.sh for the make idf-* targets. make idf-build # idf.py -D IDF_TARGET=esp32 build make idf-flash # flash over USB; make idf-flash IDF_PORT=/dev/ttyACM0 make idf-monitor # the serial monitor (leave with Ctrl+]) make idf-size # the size report of the firmware make bundle # build everything and collect dist/ for distribution A first checkout needs the target once. With ESP-IDF exported: idf.py set-target esp32 idf.py build idf.py -p /dev/ttyACM0 flash monitor idf.py menuconfig # the Micro OS Kconfig (components/drivers/Kconfig) idf.py erase-flash # wipes everything, MicroFS data included The board is on /dev/ttyACM0 and the port belongs to the group uucp : sudo gpasswd -a $USER uucp # log out and back in afterwards tools/device-test.sh builds, flashes and reads the console, and prints RESULT: PASS when the self test, the hardware doctor and the shell are up. The layout of the flash is in partitions.csv : two application slots of 1.125 MiB, 132 KiB of programs in progs and 5.56 MiB of MicroFS (ADR 0022). The board's own README is docs/ports/esp32/README.md , the pins and quirks are in docs/ports/esp32/hardware.md . The checks around the builds ¶ make integrity # the bundle, the image headers, the partition table, git, hygiene, format make format # reformat the C sources with clang-format make ci # build, test, test-asan, test-tsan, smoke, [x86-smoke], integrity make ci runs the x86-64 smoke test when qemu-system-x86_64 is on PATH and says so when it is not. It does not build the firmware, and it does not run the VGA or disk smoke tests or the device test: those are separate commands. testing.md explains what each check proves. When the build stops ¶ troubleshooting.md is the table of the errors that happen most: ESP-IDF not found, a toolchain that the registry of ESP-IDF does not know, a QEMU without a display, /dev/ttyACM0 that belongs to somebody else, and the link errors of a stale build directory. docs.text: Files ¶ Micro OS has one filesystem of its own, MicroFS , two virtual filesystems, a FAT12/16/32 volume it can both read and write, and an ext2 volume it can read. The root / is MicroFS on a block device; /proc and /dev are generated by the kernel. Everything a person writes at the console lands in MicroFS unless a FAT volume is mounted, and the configuration of /etc has a second copy in the store of the port, which is why a format does not have to lose it. The layout of the volume, the sections and the flags of a record are described in docs/memory.md ; this page is about using it. The tree after a boot ¶ The simulator, right after a boot (the board adds /log ; x86-64 has the same tree and adds /bin with the programs of its disk image): microos> tree / / |-- etc/ | |-- console | |-- display | |-- font | `-- init.d/ |-- proc/ | |-- version | |-- uptime | |-- meminfo | |-- tasks | |-- modules | |-- self/ | |-- 1/ | `-- ... `-- dev/ |-- tty0 `-- ... Path What it is / MicroFS on the volume of the port /etc the configuration: a file name is the key and its content the value for a single setting, key=value lines for a system ( display , font , console ) /etc/init.d the scripts of the init process, one command per line /etc/fstab the volumes the boot mounts after the root, when the file is there /proc the kernel: version , uptime , meminfo , tasks , modules , one directory per task /dev the devices: tty0 , null , input and the ones the port adds /log on the board: start.log , the log of the boot /bin on x86-64: the programs of the disk image ( hello , crash , fork , ...), written by make x86-disk and read by execve ; no boot installs them ls prints the names of a directory, one per line; -l adds the mode, the owner, the size and the date, and -a the two names . and .. . tree draws the levels below a path, and stat is the detailed view of one object. MicroFS ¶ MicroFS is a consumer of blocks, not of a flash chip: the device under it is described by kernel/blockdev.h and registered by the port. On the board it is the mfs partition of the internal flash ( flash0 , 5.56 MiB); in the simulator a file of the host ( file0 , 512 KB by default); on x86-64 the first partition of the ATA disk ( ata0p1 ) when one is attached, and a volume in the RAM ( ram0 , 512 KB) when it is not. A volume has three sections and a block is 1 KiB: Section Holds DATA the content of the files META the table of the records and the map of the free blocks INFO the header of the volume and the root record, in the last erase sector A record of today is 32 bytes: it keeps the type of the object, its mode and its owner in the upper bits of flags , and the two moments of a change ( mtime and ctime ) in the seconds of Unix after them. A volume of an older release has 16-byte records with no room for a time and mounts unchanged; its objects report zero, which is "unknown" (ADR 0013). Moving a 0.x machine, and what a version 1 volume keeps, is in docs/migration.md . The formatter asks for 256 records ( MFS_MOUNT_RECORDS ) and sizes META from the volume; the capacity is fixed at format time and cannot grow later. There is no journal : a power cut in the middle of a write leaves whatever it leaves, and fsck -y is the way back (see mkfs and fsck ); a content that was half written is not recoverable, and the check says so ( docs/debts.md ). The calls of the filesystem take one recursive lock, so two tasks can use the volume at the same time without corrupting it: each open file keeps its position in its descriptor, and the volume itself is one piece of state behind a mutex. The codes of the filesystem are translated into the codes of the system calls in one place, components/mfs/src/mfs_vfs.c . Working with files ¶ microos> write /hello.txt one two three 14 byte(s) written to /hello.txt microos> cat /hello.txt one two three microos> mkdir /data microos> df /data blocks: 482 of 487 free (1 KB each) inodes: 1274 of 1279 free microos> rm /hello.txt write replaces the file and appends a newline; the text is one line of at most 127 bytes. rm removes a file, not a directory, and there is no -r . df prints the free blocks and inodes of the filesystem of the path. stat shows the mode, the owner and the size; chmod and chown change the first two. A program asks for the moments of a change with statx (number 26 of the ABI) and microos_statx() in the library; a volume of version 1 has none, so the two times come back as zero and not as 1970. The rules are in kernel-abi.md and in docs/syscall-abi.md : one user (uid 0), no root bypass, and a zero mode means "this record predates the modes", so chmod 000 is refused. mkfs and fsck ¶ microos> mkfs -y mkfs: the volume is formatted mkfs -y unmounts / , formats the volume and mounts it again. Without -y it does nothing but print its usage; with -y everything in MicroFS is gone. The attributes are the ones of the inode, not zeros: stat , statx and ls -l report the nine bits of i_mode , the uid of the owner and the moments of the change: microos> mount ata0p1 /mnt/linux ext2 mount: ata0p1 is mounted at /mnt/linux microos> ls -l /mnt/linux -rw-r--r-- 1000 11 21 Nov 12:00 hello.txt drwxr-xr-x root 1024 21 Nov 12:00 sub/ microos> cat /mnt/linux/hello.txt hello ext2 microos> df -h /mnt/linux /mnt/linux: 63.9 MB total, 7.4 MB free The volume is read-only . write , mkdir , unlink , chmod and chown answer ENOTSUP , and an open that asks for O_WRONLY , O_RDWR , O_CREAT , O_TRUNC or O_APPEND is refused at the door: the reader never touches the medium and never asks the device to sync. A journal is not replayed, so an ext3 or ext4 volume is refused with ENOTSUP ; a link is reported but not followed. No access time , so statx has two moments of three; a read does not rewrite a record. The options of /etc/fstab are not acted on : only defaults is accepted, and a volume mounted at the console is not written back to the table. MicroFS is one volume at a time : the type mfs mounts the medium the filesystem keeps, so a second MicroFS volume is a change of the filesystem. No journal under a write : fsck -y repairs the damage that the medium of MicroFS or of FAT explains, and leaves what it cannot prove for a person; the data of a write that was in flight is not recovered. No mv , no cp : rm -r and the other commands of the shell are there. One user , so the owner of a file is a number that is stored and checked but not a second party. docs.text: Micro OS has one filesystem of its own, MicroFS , two virtual filesystems, a FAT12/16/32 volume it can both read and write, and an ext2 volume it can read. The root / is MicroFS on a block device; /proc and /dev are generated by the kernel. Everything a person writes at the console lands in MicroFS unless a FAT volume is mounted, and the configuration of /etc has a second copy in the store of the port, which is why a format does not have to lose it. The layout of the volume, the sections and the flags of a record are described in docs/memory.md ; this page is about using it.

docs.text: MicroFS is a consumer of blocks, not of a flash chip: the device under it is described by kernel/blockdev.h and registered by the port. On the board it is the mfs partition of the internal flash ( flash0 , 5.56 MiB); in the simulator a file of the host ( file0 , 512 KB by default); on x86-64 the first partition of the ATA disk ( ata0p1 ) when one is attached, and a volume in the RAM ( ram0 , 512 KB) when it is not. A volume has three sections and a block is 1 KiB: Section Holds DATA the content of the files META the table of the records and the map of the free blocks INFO the header of the volume and the root record, in the last erase sector A record of today is 32 bytes: it keeps the type of the object, its mode and its owner in the upper bits of flags , and the two moments of a change ( mtime and ctime ) in the seconds of Unix after them. A volume of an older release has 16-byte records with no room for a time and mounts unchanged; its objects report zero, which is "unknown" (ADR 0013). Moving a 0.x machine, and what a version 1 volume keeps, is in docs/migration.md . The formatter asks for 256 records ( MFS_MOUNT_RECORDS ) and sizes META from the volume; the capacity is fixed at format time and cannot grow later. There is no journal : a power cut in the middle of a write leaves whatever it leaves, and fsck -y is the way back (see mkfs and fsck ); a content that was half written is not recoverable, and the check says so ( docs/debts.md ). The calls of the filesystem take one recursive lock, so two tasks can use the volume at the same time without corrupting it: each open file keeps its position in its descriptor, and the volume itself is one piece of state behind a mutex. The codes of the filesystem are translated into the codes of the system calls in one place, components/mfs/src/mfs_vfs.c .

The mount does not ask whether the medium can be written: a card with its physical write switch on mounts and is refused at the first write, because reading it is still useful. Writes go to the medium before the call returns and the device is synced when it has a sync of its own, but there is no journal : a power cut in the middle of a write can leave a cluster no chain names or a half-written entry. fsck fat <point|device> walks the volume: the boot sector and the BPB, the copies of the table, the chains, the entries and their long names, and the clusters no chain names. Without a flag it only reports, and a damaged volume is left the way it was found so that it can be copied off the medium first. With -y the safe repairs are applied and the check runs again; the rules are in the section above , and what the medium cannot explain is left and named. That is the price of writing a volume this kernel did not format, and it is written in docs/debts.md . The host test mounts MicroFS at / and FAT at /mnt/fat at the same time, reads and writes through the VFS, and mounts the same image again after an unmount to prove the bytes are on the medium. On a board or an x86-64 image the type is registered at the boot when MICRO_OS_FS_FAT32 is on; the board has it off by default. MicroFS registers its own type ( mfs ) as well, so the volume of the flash can be named like any other.
docs.title: The second filesystem

docs.text: components/fs_ext2 is a second reader of a format of the world, and the first one with inodes ( ADR 0019 ). The type is ext2 ; the component is behind MICRO_OS_FS_EXT2 , off by default on the board and on x86-64, and linked by the host build and its tests. The reader walks the superblock at byte 1024, the table of the group descriptors, the inode table of every group, the twelve direct blocks of an inode and one, two or three levels of indirection. A directory is a stream of records of a variable length, the names are compared byte for byte (ext2 is case sensitive) and a name of up to 255 bytes is found whole even when the listing cuts it at the 32 bytes of struct vfs_dirent . A hole of a sparse file reads as zeros. The attributes are the ones of the inode, not zeros: stat , statx and ls -l report the nine bits of i_mode , the uid of the owner and the moments of the change: microos> mount ata0p1 /mnt/linux ext2 mount: ata0p1 is mounted at /mnt/linux microos> ls -l /mnt/linux -rw-r--r-- 1000 11 21 Nov 12:00 hello.txt drwxr-xr-x root 1024 21 Nov 12:00 sub/ microos> cat /mnt/linux/hello.txt hello ext2 microos> df -h /mnt/linux /mnt/linux: 63.9 MB total, 7.4 MB free The volume is read-only . write , mkdir , unlink , chmod and chown answer ENOTSUP , and an open that asks for O_WRONLY , O_RDWR , O_CREAT , O_TRUNC or O_APPEND is refused at the door: the reader never touches the medium and never asks the device to sync. A journal is not replayed, so an ext3 or ext4 volume is refused with ENOTSUP ; a link is reported but not followed. A damaged volume is described as it is: a superblock or a geometry that cannot be walked is EINVAL , a block or an inode outside the volume is EIO . The tests build the image themselves - a superblock, one group, a table of inodes, two directories and a file that uses all three levels of indirection around a hole - and mount it next to MicroFS; mke2fs is not a dependency of the suite. The board's boot does not register the type yet, which is in docs/debts.md .
docs.title: The third filesystem: ext2

docs.text: mount without a word lists the points of the tree, in the order the boot mounted them. With the three words device point type it mounts a volume of a registered type; umount gives the point back: microos> mount / /mnt/fat microos> mount ata0p1 /mnt/fat fat32 mount: ata0p1 is mounted at /mnt/fat microos> ls /mnt/fat ... microos> umount /mnt/fat umount: /mnt/fat is out of the tree The point need not exist in the filesystem above it, and neither does its parent: a mount is shown in the listing of the directory above, which is how /proc , /dev and /mnt/fat appear in ls . What is already there has to be a directory, so a mount over a file is not a directory ; a point that already holds another filesystem is device or resource busy , and a point with a mount below it stays until the smaller one leaves. / is the exception: the mounts of /proc and /dev do not live on its volume, so mkfs -y may take the root out while they stay.
docs.title: Mounting a volume

docs.text: The boot mounts the volumes of /etc/fstab after the root, when the file is there. Each line is device point type [options] , # starts a comment and an empty line is not a line: # the volumes of the machine: the device, the point and the type vfsfat0 /mnt/fat fat32 # a line of Linux with the options of a mount is read as well ata0p1 /mnt/card fat32 defaults Only defaults is a known option for now: an option that the kernel cannot honour ( ro , a comma-separated list) is named in the log and its line is skipped. A line that does not mount for any other reason - a type the image does not have, a device that is not there, a point that is busy - is skipped the same way: a broken table does not stop the boot, and the shell still starts with mount -a to read it again after a repair. The file lives in MicroFS, so it is one of the files of /etc that the store of the port keeps across a format. A volume mounted at the console is not written back to the table: mount changes the tree, not the configuration.
docs.title: /etc/fstab

docs.text: A few settings are files of /etc : the name of the machine, the console, the table of the mounts. The systems of parameters - /etc/display with rotation=90 , /etc/font with scale=1 , /etc/console with theme=dark - are one file per system, with key=value lines and comments; the boot applies them before the first frame, and a key the machine cannot honour is kept and ignored with a warning ( ADR 0021 ). microos> cat /etc/display # the screen rotation=0 invert=1 brightness=100 theme=dark microos> config set display.rotation 90 display.rotation=90 microos> config get display.rotation display.rotation=90 The files stay data of the volume: cat , write and config edit them, and the store of the port brings them back after a format. The keys, the defaults, the limits of a file and the table of what each machine honours are in settings.md .
docs.title: The settings of a machine

docs.text: No write to an ext2 volume, and no journal under a FAT write. A FAT volume is written without a log; a second FAT volume and a mount of a card at runtime are ahead. fsck fat -y repairs the damage the medium explains (lost clusters, a loop, a cross-link, a size against its chain), but the boot sector, two copies of the table that differ and a directory whose head is shared are left for a person. ext2 is a reader: a write, a new name, a mode or an owner is ENOTSUP , a journal is not replayed, and there is no fsck ext2 - e2fsck is the tool of that format. No access time , so statx has two moments of three; a read does not rewrite a record. The options of /etc/fstab are not acted on : only defaults is accepted, and a volume mounted at the console is not written back to the table. MicroFS is one volume at a time : the type mfs mounts the medium the filesystem keeps, so a second MicroFS volume is a change of the filesystem. No journal under a write : fsck -y repairs the damage that the medium of MicroFS or of FAT explains, and leaves what it cannot prove for a person; the data of a write that was in flight is not recovered. No mv , no cp : rm -r and the other commands of the shell are there. One user , so the owner of a file is a number that is stored and checked but not a second party. No mv , no cp : rm -r and the other commands of the shell are there. One user , so the owner of a file is a number that is stored and checked but not a second party. docs.text: Start here ¶ Micro OS is a Linux-like kernel for small machines. One portable core lives in components/kernel/ ; every machine is a port under it, and a board is a description of a machine plus the drivers of its chips. The same sources build as a Linux process (the unit tests and the simulator), as a bare-metal x86-64 machine in QEMU, and as the firmware of the M5Stack StickC Plus2. It is Linux- like , not Linux: the system calls are the same shape, the filesystem and the shell are the same shape, but there is no MMU on the board, no multi-user, and no dynamic linker. The x86-64 port has an MMU and uses it: a program runs in ring 3 in its own address space. The honest list of the differences is in docs/architecture.md , section 2. One kernel, four ports ¶ Port What it is Documentation ESP32 the StickC Plus2: ESP-IDF, FreeRTOS, lwIP, NVS docs/ports/esp32 x86-64 bare metal in QEMU: its own loader, ring 3 docs/ports/x86_64 host a Linux process: the tests and the simulator docs/ports/host null no machine at all: linked by the checks docs/ports/null The board is one port of several, not the project. The boundary is a contract with a version ( kernel/port/*.h , 1.8 in this tree), checked at the boot and by make integrity ; ADR 0004 explains why. What you need ¶ Need For Note cmake , ninja , gcc , python3 every host check any current Linux distribution qemu-system-x86_64 the x86-64 port optional; without it the machine is only built ESP-IDF v5.3 the firmware of the board only for make idf-* ; see build.md clang-format is needed by make format and by the format check of make integrity ; valgrind and pyserial are optional. The whole list with the packages of Arch is in commands.md . The first ten minutes ¶ From the root of the repository: make test # build the host and run the unit tests (and the null probe) make sim # boot the whole system as a process, on a volume in a file make sim is interactive: it boots the kernel, brings up MicroFS on a file volume, /proc , /dev , the configuration of /etc , the init scripts and the shell. The transcript starts like this (the version and the build date are the ones of your tree): MicroOS 0.5.0-rc1 (build ...) board: host_sim - Micro OS host simulator arch: x86_64, compiler: gcc ... port: host, contract 1.9 [ ok ] sched file0: 512 sector(s) of 1024 bytes on /tmp/microos-sim.img sim: the volume is /tmp/microos-sim.img (512 KB) [ ok ] storage ... MicroOS shell ready. Type 'help' for the list of commands. microos> Then type a few commands; leaving the input (Ctrl+D in a terminal, or the end of a pipe) ends the run: microos> uname MicroOS 0.5.0-rc1 x86_64 (build ...) microos> tree / / |-- etc/ | `-- init.d/ |-- proc/ ... microos> fsck fsck: 0 file(s), 3 directory(ies), 484 of 487 block(s) free fsck: the volume is consistent make smoke drives the same simulator with a scripted list of commands and checks the transcript; it is the end-to-end test of the host build. The other two machines ¶ The x86-64 port is the one that proves the kernel is portable, and the only machine that runs a program out of a file: make x86-build # the loader, the kernel image and the programs, in build-x86/ make x86-disk # build-x86/programs.img: /bin and /etc of MicroFS make x86-run # a QEMU window: VGA text and the PS/2 keyboard make x86-run-serial # the same machine on the serial console (-nographic) make x86-smoke # boot it and check the transcript, without a window The machine boots from the disk image: /bin (sixteen programs) and /etc are objects of a MicroFS volume that make x86-disk writes with the host tool tools/mkfs_mfs.c , and the boot mounts the volume and runs /bin/hello through execve . The tree is the tree of the other ports - /bin , /etc , /proc and /dev - so tree / shows the same shape here as on the board and in the simulator. The window needs a QEMU built with a display backend (the GTK one is a package of its own in some distributions); build.md has the package names and the fallbacks. make x86-run-disk keeps a disk of its own between runs ( build-x86/disk.img ), so a file written at the console is there after a reset; make x86-run and make x86-smoke start from a fresh build of the image every time. The board: make idf-build # the firmware (ESP-IDF v5.3) make idf-flash # over USB; IDF_PORT=/dev/ttyACM0 when it is not found tools/device-test.sh # build, flash, read the console, print RESULT: PASS The board comes up with the self test, the hardware doctor, the shell on the UART and a copy of it on the TFT, telnet on port 23, and the commands of the drivers ( battery , display , input , mic , wifi , ...). Where to go next ¶ build.md - the three builds in detail, and the errors that stop them. shell.md - the command line, the commands and what they print. files.md - where /etc lives, how mkfs and fsck behave. programs.md - what exec needs and which machine can run it. ports.md - the differences between the four machines at a glance. What this is not yet ¶ A short list, so that nothing here reads as a promise: No MMU on the board, no memory protection. The user/kernel split is logical; fork() shares the memory of the parent and re-enters the program. A .mox on the board runs as a task in the kernel's address space, and a bad pointer reboots the machine. Programs need a machine that can enter them. x86-64 does it with ring 3 and page tables; the board runs an Xtensa .mox without protection; the simulator and the null port answer ENOSYS , because jumping into an arbitrary image inside the test process is not a promise the host can keep. One user, uid 0. A file has a mode and an owner, and the mode is checked, but there is no group and no second user. No TLS, and the network is the LAN. HTTP, MQTT and telnet are plain text; there is no HTTPS, no certificate store, no IPv6 and no raw sockets, and httpd and telnet take no password. Keep the machine on the network of its owner ( SECURITY.md ). FAT32 is read and written, ext2 is read-only. MicroFS is the root of the tree; a build can also carry FAT12/16/32 ( ADR 0009 ) and mount it beside MicroFS, and it can read an ext2 volume with its modes, its owner and its moments ( ADR 0019 ). MicroFS keeps the two moments of a change and no journal; FAT keeps no time yet, and a writable ext2 and a second FAT volume are still ahead. docs/debts.md keeps the full register with the next step of each row. docs/roadmap.md is the plan. docs.text: Kernel and ABI ¶ The system calls are the only door between a program and the kernel. Their numbers are a contract : they are written down, covered by a test, and never change. A program built for one version of the kernel keeps working with the next one. The canonical document, with the arguments and the reasoning, is docs/syscall-abi.md ; this page is the map for a person who wants to use the system, not a second copy of the contract. The table ¶ No. Call What it does 0 exit end the task (or the program) with a status 1 read bytes out of a descriptor 2 write bytes into a descriptor 3 open a descriptor for a path, with flags 4 close drop a descriptor 5 stat the type, the mode, the owner, the size 6 lseek move the position of a descriptor 7 unlink remove a file 8 mkdir create a directory 9 readdir the next entries of a directory 10 getpid the number of the task 11 getcwd the current directory 12 ioctl a command of a device 13 yield give the processor away 14 sleep wait in milliseconds 15 uptime milliseconds since the boot 16 reboot restart the machine 17 fork a child task 18 getppid the number of the parent 19 waitpid wait for a child, get its status 20 malloc memory of the kernel heap 21 free give it back 22 realloc resize a block 23 chmod the mode of an object 24 chown the owner of an object 25 execve make the caller a program, with its arguments and environment 26 statx the numbers of stat and the moments of a change 27 pipe two descriptors of one pipe 28 dup2 a second descriptor of an open file 29 kill send a signal to a task 30 signal install a handler, get the previous one 31 sigreturn return from a handler (the port's page, not a program) 32 getlimit the current memory, CPU or descriptor limit of the task 33 setlimit lower one of them 34 is the count, not a call. A number that is not in the table is ENOSYS ; a new call always takes the next free number, and an old one never moves. The shell prints the same table with abi : microos> abi the system calls of the kernel: nr name 0 exit ... 25 execve 26 statx 27 pipe 28 dup2 29 kill 30 signal 31 sigreturn 32 getlimit 33 setlimit 34 call(s) registered The convention is the one of Linux: the number and six arguments, the result in the return value, and a negative result is an error with the number of POSIX ( -14 is EFAULT , -2 is ENOENT , -38 is ENOSYS ). The width of an argument is the width of a pointer of the machine: 32 bits on the board, 64 bits on the host and on x86-64. The edge of the table ¶ Every argument is checked where it enters, in components/kernel/src/ksys.c , before a filesystem or a driver sees it: a path is not NULL, begins at / , and ends within 127 characters ( KSYS_PATH_MAX , one less than VFS_PATH_MAX ); a path that does not end in the window is ENAMETOOLONG ; a buffer is NULL only with a zero length, and no call touches more than 64 KiB in one exchange; a longer one is E2BIG , a NULL with a length is EINVAL ; the memory of the caller is checked through the port: on a machine with paging the kernel walks the page tables of the program, and a range that is not there is EFAULT ; the bytes are then copied with copy_from_user() / copy_to_user() , so the VFS never sees a pointer of the program; the flags of open are one of the three access modes and no bit outside the contract; the whence of lseek and the pid of waitpid are compared before a cast can cut a wide register into a valid value; stat and getcwd need the place for the answer: NULL is EINVAL , a place that is not the caller's memory is EFAULT ; readdir takes whole entries: a count that is not a multiple of the size of an entry is EINVAL . EFAULT is the most interesting of them, because it is what a machine with an MMU can finally say. On x86-64 the null page, the guard page under the stack, the part of the window that was never mapped and a range that runs past 0x03000000 are all "not there": the call answers -14 instead of taking a page fault in ring 0. /bin/badptr is the program of that test - it hands write , stat and read a pointer outside the window, a range that crosses its end and the guard page, and every call answers 14 while the machine goes on and writes a line with a valid pointer afterwards. Signals ¶ Four signals, the numbers of POSIX: SIGINT (2), SIGPIPE (13), SIGTERM (15) and SIGCHLD (17). signal(sig, handler) installs a function of the program and answers the previous disposition; SIG_DFL ends a task that gets INT , TERM or PIPE with the status 128 + the signal, SIG_IGN throws the signal away, and SIGCHLD is ignored by default. kill(pid, sig) sends a signal to one task with a positive pid; 0 and -1 are not groups here, and a pid that names no task is ESRCH ( -3 , the number the table already used for "file exists"). A signal is answered in the context of the task that gets it, on the way out of a system call or on the tick of the timer of x86-64. A handler of a program runs in ring 3: the port puts a frame below the stack pointer of the program and the program returns through the restorer page, which calls sigreturn (29). A handler of a task of the host or of the board is an ordinary function of the kernel and runs in place. waitpid() looks at a finished child first and then at the signals; a pending signal that has to be answered makes the call answer EINTR and leaves the child to the next wait. The exit of a child marks SIGCHLD on its parent. No job control: the system has no groups and no & , fg or bg ; Ctrl+C while the shell runs a program sends SIGINT to that program, and while it runs a pipeline to every stage of it and the programs they started (the job of ADR 0017). kill takes a pid from ps . ADR 0015 has the design, and the x86-64 smoke test runs /bin/signals through all of it. Descriptors ¶ Every task has a table of four descriptors, and the descriptor is the number of the slot. The open file behind it is a counted description of the kernel: two descriptors of one task ( dup2 ) and the copies of the parent and the child of a fork name one open file, with one position and one set of flags. A descriptor remembers the access it was opened with: reading one opened for writing, or writing one opened for reading, is EBADF before a filesystem is asked. The position lives in the description, so two tasks that opened their own files do not move each other's cursor. A directory is opened with KSYS_O_DIRECTORY ( 0x0800 ) and read with readdir ; it is read, never written. A plain open of a directory is EISDIR , and readdir of a file is ENOTDIR . pipe(fds) (27) gives two ordinary descriptors, fds[0] reading and fds[1] writing; the pipe is a ring of 256 bytes in the kernel. The end of the writing end is the end of the file (a read gives 0), and a write with no reader is EPIPE - there is no SIGPIPE yet, so the error is the whole answer. A wait of a pipe is a poll with a bound of half a second and then EAGAIN ; lseek of a pipe is ESPIPE and readdir is ENOTDIR . dup2(oldfd, newfd) (28) makes newfd a second descriptor of one open file, closes what was open there, and answers newfd ; a number outside the table is EBADF . ADR 0014 has the design and the limits. Limits ¶ A task starts with the ceiling of three resources and may only lower them: the memory it holds (2 MiB), the processor time it spends (about 49 days) and the descriptors it opens (4). setlimit (33) takes a selector ( KSYS_RLIMIT_MEMORY , _CPU , _FDS ) and a value; getlimit (32) copies the current limit to the caller. A raise is EPERM : there is one user, uid 0, and it gets no exemption, so a program cannot lift its own ceiling. The memory is the sum of the user blocks of the task - the kernel and the system utilities are not charged - and a block over it is 0 from malloc ( ENOMEM from the library); free returns the room. The CPU time is counted at the system calls and at the tick of the port; when it reaches the limit the task is marked with SIGTERM (the closest of the four signals to SIGXCPU ) and the default action ends it with 143. The descriptors stop at the limit with EMFILE : open , pipe and a dup2 onto a number at or above it. Lowering a limit never closes what is already open. The library has microos_getlimit , microos_setlimit and microos_getrlimits , the shell has ulimit to print and lower the limits of the shell, and docs/syscall-abi.md has the contract. The mode and the owner ¶ Every object has nine bits of rwx and a uid of fifteen bits, stored in the spare bits of its MicroFS record ( docs/memory.md ). A new file is 0644 , a new directory 0755 , and the owner is 0. The system has one user , uid 0, and it gets no exemption of root : a file of mode 0200 cannot be read by the only user of the system either. An object owned by uid 0 is judged by the triad of the owner, one owned by any other number by the triad of the others, because there is no group here. open compares its access with the mode before a descriptor exists, so every filesystem answers a forbidden open the same way ( EPERM ); execve needs the x bit; stat reports and checks nothing, as in POSIX. A mode outside the nine bits and an owner outside the fifteen are EINVAL , not a number cut to fit. chmod 000 is not expressible: a zero in the record means "this record predates the modes", so the filesystem refuses it instead of writing a number it would read back as 0644 . docs.text: The system calls are the only door between a program and the kernel. Their numbers are a contract : they are written down, covered by a test, and never change. A program built for one version of the kernel keeps working with the next one. The canonical document, with the arguments and the reasoning, is docs/syscall-abi.md ; this page is the map for a person who wants to use the system, not a second copy of the contract.

docs.text: No. Call What it does 0 exit end the task (or the program) with a status 1 read bytes out of a descriptor 2 write bytes into a descriptor 3 open a descriptor for a path, with flags 4 close drop a descriptor 5 stat the type, the mode, the owner, the size 6 lseek move the position of a descriptor 7 unlink remove a file 8 mkdir create a directory 9 readdir the next entries of a directory 10 getpid the number of the task 11 getcwd the current directory 12 ioctl a command of a device 13 yield give the processor away 14 sleep wait in milliseconds 15 uptime milliseconds since the boot 16 reboot restart the machine 17 fork a child task 18 getppid the number of the parent 19 waitpid wait for a child, get its status 20 malloc memory of the kernel heap 21 free give it back 22 realloc resize a block 23 chmod the mode of an object 24 chown the owner of an object 25 execve make the caller a program, with its arguments and environment 26 statx the numbers of stat and the moments of a change 27 pipe two descriptors of one pipe 28 dup2 a second descriptor of an open file 29 kill send a signal to a task 30 signal install a handler, get the previous one 31 sigreturn return from a handler (the port's page, not a program) 32 getlimit the current memory, CPU or descriptor limit of the task 33 setlimit lower one of them 34 is the count, not a call. docs.text: Every argument is checked where it enters, in components/kernel/src/ksys.c , before a filesystem or a driver sees it: a path is not NULL, begins at / , and ends within 127 characters ( KSYS_PATH_MAX , one less than VFS_PATH_MAX ); a path that does not end in the window is ENAMETOOLONG ; a buffer is NULL only with a zero length, and no call touches more than 64 KiB in one exchange; a longer one is E2BIG , a NULL with a length is EINVAL ; the memory of the caller is checked through the port: on a machine with paging the kernel walks the page tables of the program, and a range that is not there is EFAULT ; the bytes are then copied with copy_from_user() / copy_to_user() , so the VFS never sees a pointer of the program; the flags of open are one of the three access modes and no bit outside the contract; the whence of lseek and the pid of waitpid are compared before a cast can cut a wide register into a valid value; stat and getcwd need the place for the answer: NULL is EINVAL , a place that is not the caller's memory is EFAULT ; readdir takes whole entries: a count that is not a multiple of the size of an entry is EINVAL . EFAULT is the most interesting of them, because it is what a machine with an MMU can finally say. docs.text: Four signals, the numbers of POSIX: SIGINT (2), SIGPIPE (13), SIGTERM (15) and SIGCHLD (17). signal(sig, handler) installs a function of the program and answers the previous disposition; SIG_DFL ends a task that gets INT , TERM or PIPE with the status 128 + the signal, SIG_IGN throws the signal away, and SIGCHLD is ignored by default. kill(pid, sig) sends a signal to one task with a positive pid; 0 and -1 are not groups here, and a pid that names no task is ESRCH ( -3 , the number the table already used for "file exists"). A signal is answered in the context of the task that gets it, on the way out of a system call or on the tick of the timer of x86-64. A handler of a program runs in ring 3: the port puts a frame below the stack pointer of the program and the program returns through the restorer page, which calls sigreturn (29). A handler of a task of the host or of the board is an ordinary function of the kernel and runs in place. waitpid() looks at a finished child first and then at the signals; a pending signal that has to be answered makes the call answer EINTR and leaves the child to the next wait. The exit of a child marks SIGCHLD on its parent. No job control: the system has no groups and no & , fg or bg ; Ctrl+C while the shell runs a program sends SIGINT to that program, and while it runs a pipeline to every stage of it and the programs they started (the job of ADR 0017). kill takes a pid from ps . ADR 0015 has the design, and the x86-64 smoke test runs /bin/signals through all of it.

docs.text: Every task has a table of four descriptors, and the descriptor is the number of the slot. The open file behind it is a counted description of the kernel: two descriptors of one task ( dup2 ) and the copies of the parent and the child of a fork name one open file, with one position and one set of flags. A descriptor remembers the access it was opened with: reading one opened for writing, or writing one opened for reading, is EBADF before a filesystem is asked. The position lives in the description, so two tasks that opened their own files do not move each other's cursor. A directory is opened with KSYS_O_DIRECTORY ( 0x0800 ) and read with readdir ; it is read, never written. docs.text: The network ¶ Micro OS speaks the network with the sockets of its port: the board has WiFi and lwIP, x86-64 has a virtio-net card and a small stack of its own, and the host substrate uses the sockets of Linux. The kernel does not know which: kernel/port/net.h is a socket, a name and a byte, and the client of HTTP and the resolver of names live above it. What a machine has today ¶ ESP32 (board) x86-64 (QEMU) host substrate link WiFi station, lwIP virtio-net the sockets of Linux address DHCP from the access point static 10.0.2.15/24 , gateway 10.0.2.2 , DNS 10.0.2.3 (the user network of QEMU) whatever Linux gives names lwIP ( getaddrinfo ) a resolver of its own with a cache: dns <name> the resolver of Linux TCP and UDP yes yes yes ICMP the stack of lwIP ping <address> no HTTP client http get <url> no command yet tests only HTTP server httpd [port\|off] , the page of the state no command yet no NTP ntp [server] no command yet no MQTT mqtt <host> <port> <topic> <message> , QoS 0 not built no telnet telnet [on\|off] , the shell on port 23 no no The commands of x86-64 are netinfo (the device, the address, the counters), ping , netudp (one exchange) and dns . make x86-net-smoke boots the machine with a card of QEMU and checks the stack: ARP, ICMP, UDP, a client and a server of TCP, and the cache of the resolver. The HTTP client of the board ¶ http get is a client of a console, not of a file: microos> http get http://example.com/ 200, 1256 byte(s) <!doctype html>... It speaks HTTP/1.0, reads the answer into a buffer, and cuts a body that is longer than the buffer ( components/net/src/http.c ). There is no chunked body, no redirect and no TLS, and the answer of a server is a line of text for a person, not a program to install. The server is the other direction: httpd publishes the page of the state on port 80, without authentication; telnet puts the shell on port 23 and is off until a person turns it on. Both are described in shell.md . The stream, and what it changes ¶ K12 ( ADR 0024 ) turns the console client into a stream: Content-Length and a chunked body, a bounded number of redirects, a timeout, and a sink that is a file or the inactive slot of an update. The console face is: microos> wget http://mirror.example/hello-x86_64.mox /var/cache/pkg/hello.mox hello-x86_64.mox: 8 192 bytes, 2.1 KB/s, done The same stream fills the inactive slot of the board, which is the update over the network that 1.1 left open. The public internet is HTTPS. TLS is mbedTLS : the board takes the copy of ESP-IDF, and x86-64 vendors it with a freestanding platform layer - the allocator of the kernel, entropy from RDRAND , the clock from NTP and the roots of /etc/ssl/certs.pem through the VFS. A clock that NTP has not set is a warning at the handshake, because a certificate has dates. A package is trusted by its signature , not by its transport: TLS protects the wire, and the Ed25519 trailer of the file protects the program. A hostile mirror can refuse to serve; it cannot replace the bytes. What is not there yet ¶ no TLS on either machine: the handshake is the work of K12; no HTTP client and no NTP command on x86-64 (the network of the port is TCP, UDP, ICMP and DNS; the console client is the work of K12); no DHCP and no IPv6 on x86-64: the address of the port is the one of the user network of QEMU, and a real link is a later change; no congestion window and no retransmission timers beyond the simple ones of the port ( docs/ports/x86_64/README.md says what the stack is). The network of a machine without a link - the simulator and the host substrate - is the sockets of Linux for the tests, and nothing for the console.

docs.text: pkg : programs from a repository ¶ pkg is the installer of x86-64. It brings a program from a repository of its own ( microos-progs ), checks its signature and puts it in /usr/bin . It is the second half of the promise of 2.0 - a machine a person changes from the machine itself; the settings of /etc were the first. Status: planned for 1.2. 1.1.0 has no pkg ; a program is a file a person writes or copies. The contract of the command is ADR 0024 §6. The shape of a package ¶ A repository publishes an index and the files it names: index.json name, version, machine, abi, size, sha-256 hello-x86_64.mox the program hello-x86_64.sig its Ed25519 signature The index is signed with the same key as the images of the system ( ADR 0020 ). A package names the machine (the MOX1 header) and the ABI of the kernel it needs; a package for another machine, or for a newer ABI, does not install. The commands ¶ The console Short What it does pkg sync -Sy refresh the index of every repository pkg upgrade -Su a newer version of every installed package pkg sync --upgrade -Syu both, in that order pkg install NAME... -S fetch, verify and install pkg install ./x.mox -U the same for a file on the machine pkg remove NAME... -R remove; -Rn also the files it owns pkg search TERM -Ss the name and the summary of a match pkg info NAME -Si / -Qi the package in a repository / installed pkg list -Q the installed packages; -Qe only the explicit ones pkg files NAME -Ql the files a package installed pkg check -Qk the digest of every installed file pkg clean -Sc the cache, keeping what an install needs pkg repo add URL a repository and its key, in /etc/pkg.conf pkg log what was installed, removed and when microos> pkg -Syu :: refreshing the index of microos-progs :: 3 package(s) in the index :: upgrade hello 1.0.0 -> 1.1.0 :: download hello-1.1.0-x86_64.mox: 8 192 bytes, done :: signature ok, installing /usr/bin/hello microos> pkg -Ss editor microos-progs/vi 1.2.0 a small screen editor microos> pkg -S vi The flags of an install ¶ --noconfirm , --needed (a version already there is a no-op), --download-only , --dry-run (the plan, not a byte written), --allow-downgrade (a warning; the default refuses an older version), --ignore NAME , --force (reinstall), --offline (the cache only), --root DIR (a volume, for the tests), --repo NAME , --cachedir DIR , --color auto|always|never , --quiet , --verbose , and NAME=VERSION for a pin. --help prints the table and pkg --version the version of the tool. There is no --nosignature . A package without a valid signature does not install, and no flag is a door around that. An install is atomic: the bytes go to NAME.mox.new , the digest and the signature are checked, the file is flushed, and a rename makes it visible ( vfs_rename , a new operation of the filesystem). A volume that cannot rename still installs, with a warning that the window is not atomic. Where it lives ¶ The database is /var/pkg , the programs are /usr/bin , the cache is /var/cache/pkg , and the repositories and their keys are /etc/pkg.conf and /etc/pkg/keys . The console face is a command of the shell at first (like config ) and a program of /usr/bin when the calls it needs - open , write , rename , unlink - are in the table of the system calls. What it does not do, and why ¶ It does not build. The convenience of yay and paru is two things: a package manager with muscle memory, and an AUR build on the machine. The first is the contract above; the second is not possible here. A program is static MOX1 , the machine has no compiler, and an install script is the code of a stranger run as root. No dependency solver. A program is static; its dependencies are the machine and the ABI, and the index names them. No scripts, no shared libraries, no delta update. A package is a file replaced whole. No installer on the board. The progs partition of the ESP32 belongs to the firmware (ADR 0018); a program of the board is a new progs.bin and a flash. A third-party repository is the answer to "I want more than the official index": pkg repo add takes a URL and its key, and the signature rule is the same. That is the freedom of the AUR without the build.

docs.text: The console Short What it does pkg sync -Sy refresh the index of every repository pkg upgrade -Su a newer version of every installed package pkg sync --upgrade -Syu both, in that order pkg install NAME... -S fetch, verify and install pkg install ./x.mox -U the same for a file on the machine pkg remove NAME... -R remove; -Rn also the files it owns pkg search TERM -Ss the name and the summary of a match pkg info NAME -Si / -Qi the package in a repository / installed pkg list -Q the installed packages; -Qe only the explicit ones pkg files NAME -Ql the files a package installed pkg check -Qk the digest of every installed file pkg clean -Sc the cache, keeping what an install needs pkg repo add URL a repository and its key, in /etc/pkg.conf pkg log what was installed, removed and when microos> pkg -Syu :: refreshing the index of microos-progs :: 3 package(s) in the index :: upgrade hello 1.0.0 -> 1.1.0 :: download hello-1.1.0-x86_64.mox: 8 192 bytes, done :: signature ok, installing /usr/bin/hello microos> pkg -Ss editor microos-progs/vi 1.2.0 a small screen editor microos> pkg -S vi

docs.text: --noconfirm , --needed (a version already there is a no-op), --download-only , --dry-run (the plan, not a byte written), --allow-downgrade (a warning; the default refuses an older version), --ignore NAME , --force (reinstall), --offline (the cache only), --root DIR (a volume, for the tests), --repo NAME , --cachedir DIR , --color auto|always|never , --quiet , --verbose , and NAME=VERSION for a pin. --help prints the table and pkg --version the version of the tool. An install is atomic: the bytes go to NAME.mox.new , the digest and the signature are checked, the file is flushed, and a rename makes it visible ( vfs_rename , a new operation of the filesystem). docs.text: It does not build. The convenience of yay and paru is two things: a package manager with muscle memory, and an AUR build on the machine. The first is the contract above; the second is not possible here. A program is static MOX1 , the machine has no compiler, and an install script is the code of a stranger run as root. No dependency solver. A program is static; its dependencies are the machine and the ABI, and the index names them. No scripts, no shared libraries, no delta update. A package is a file replaced whole. No installer on the board. The progs partition of the ESP32 belongs to the firmware (ADR 0018); a program of the board is a new progs.bin and a flash. A third-party repository is the answer to "I want more than the official index": pkg repo add takes a URL and its key, and the signature rule is the same. That is the freedom of the AUR without the build.

docs.text: Porting ¶ A port is a directory that implements the contract of components/kernel/include/kernel/port/*.h and kernel/port_task.h ; a board is the description of a machine plus the drivers of its chips. The kernel includes nothing of a platform, and make integrity fails when it tries ( ADR 0004 ). The same sources build as a Linux process, as a bare-metal x86-64 machine and as the firmware of the board because of that line. The canonical guide, with the version of the contract, every group of calls, the stubs of an absent duty and the common mistakes, is docs/porting.md . This page is the short way in; the guide and the headers are the truth. The shape of a port ¶ Group Header What the machine answers execution kernel/port_task.h stack, tasks, sleep, signals console kernel/port/console.h the bytes out, a line, a key, a poll clock kernel/port/time.h milliseconds and microseconds since the boot heap kernel/port/mem.h the internal heap, the PSRAM, alloc and free locks kernel/port/lock.h a critical section and a recursive mutex power kernel/port/power.h halt and reset identity kernel/port/info.h the name, the architecture, contract 1.9 store kernel/port/kv.h the keys behind /etc , or "nothing is stored" network kernel/port/net.h TCP client and server, one UDP exchange programs kernel/port/exec.h a window, the entry, the end, a pointer check The first seven are mandatory; the store, the network and programs may be stubs that answer honestly. The execution substrate is never optional: the scheduler has no context to switch without it. Two duties have no k_port_* call: the boot ( kernel_boot() with the board description and the subsystem table, kernel/boot.h ) and the block devices ( struct k_blockdev registered with k_blockdev_register() , kernel/blockdev.h ). Drivers are not port duties. The order that hurts least ¶ console — one character out, everything else is debugged through it; time — a counter that only goes forward; execution substrate — the kernel's own tests then run; memory — kmm and the VFS start working; locks — the critical section first, the sleeping mutex after; block device — MicroFS can mount; store, network, programs — each may say "I have none"; board and drivers. Read the existing ports in this order: ports/port_null (the shape with no machine), ports/port_host (the same calls over POSIX), ports/port_x86_64 (the bare machine, programs, signals and an MMU) and components/port_esp32 (the board). What checks it ¶ make test # the kernel against port_host, and port_null linked make integrity # [layers], [port], [budget], [sources], [format] make x86-smoke # a second machine boots tools/device-test.sh /dev/ttyACM0 # the board boots python3 tools/wiki_check.py [port] looks for every function of the contract in every port directory: the built library for the host and null ports, the sources for the ESP32 and x86-64. A boot says port: <name>, contract 1.9 ; a major mismatch panics and a minor one warns. What a port does not do ¶ It does not add a call to the contract for one board, include a driver header or know the syscall ABI. If the kernel needs a new door, that is a new call and a bump of the contract for every port — that is what the version is for. Back to the wiki index

docs.text: Ports ¶ A port is a directory that implements the contract of kernel/port/*.h on a machine; a board is a description of a machine plus the drivers of its chips. Two of the four implementations are ports - the board and x86-64; the host is the substrate of the tests and the simulator, and the null is the shape of the contract with no machine under it (ADR 0004). The kernel in components/kernel/ includes nothing of a platform, and make integrity fails when it tries. That is why the same sources build as a Linux process, as a bare-metal x86-64 machine and as the firmware of the board; the reasoning is in ADR 0004 , and the recipe for a new machine is in docs/porting.md . What runs where ¶ yes means it is there and used, - means it is absent, and a note in parentheses is the reason. ESP32 (board) x86-64 (QEMU) host (simulator) null shell UART and TFT VGA, PS/2, COM1 stdin/stdout - MicroFS the mfs partition, 5.56 MiB the disk, or 512 KB of RAM a file, 512 KB - /proc , /dev yes yes yes - /etc and its store files, NVS behind them files, no store files, a file per key - execve Xtensa code from progs , no protection ring 3, own page tables ENOSYS (a harness) ENOSYS fork() shared memory copy on write shared memory shared memory disk the internal flash ATA PIO, ata0 - - network WiFi, lwIP, telnet, HTTP, MQTT virtio-net, HTTP, httpd, DNS, MQTT is off - - panel ST7789v2 and a copy of the console VGA text a renderer into a file - MMU - (the chip has none) yes: ring 3, NX/W^X - - cores 2 under FreeRTOS, the kernel on 1 2 in the MADT, the kernel on 1 MICRO_OS_CPUS , 1 by default 1 build make idf-build make x86-build make build by the host build The matrix follows the ports, not a wish: the board has no MMU and its flash is not executable for a file, so it cannot run a program; the simulator must not jump into an arbitrary image, so it cannot either; the x86-64 machine has the loader, the page tables and the ring that make it possible. Everything else - the scheduler, the VFS, MicroFS, /proc , /dev , the libc subset, the shell - is the same code on all of them. ESP32: the board ¶ The M5Stack StickC Plus2 ( ESP32-PICO-V3-02 , 240 MHz, 2 MB PSRAM, 8 MB flash, 135x240 TFT), on ESP-IDF v5.3 and FreeRTOS. make idf-build make idf-flash IDF_PORT = /dev/ttyACM0 tools/device-test.sh /dev/ttyACM0 # build, flash, read, RESULT: PASS What works: the boot with the self test and the hardware doctor, the console on the UART and on the TFT, MicroFS on the flash, /log/start.log , the scripts of /etc/init.d , the drivers (display, buttons, buzzer, LED, IR on the pin of the LED, IMU, RTC, battery, microphone, sound detector, WiFi), deep sleep with the wake of the timer, of BUTTON C and of the RTC alarm, telnet on port 23, httpd , mqtt , http and ntp . What does not: memory protection ( fork() is the placeholder of a machine without an MMU), an update over the network (the A/B update is over USB, ADR 0022), an IR receiver (the board carries the emitter only; ir rx waits for an element on G26), the enclosure modes, a second user. The alarm of the BM8563 turns the board on from off; a sleeping board obeys it because the firmware sets the timer of the chip for the moment of the match, not because the INT of the clock is a wake line. The flash is 8 MB: two application slots of 1.125 MiB, progs 132 KiB and MicroFS 5.56 MiB (ADR 0022). The details, the pins and the quirks are in docs/ports/esp32/README.md and docs/ports/esp32/hardware.md . x86-64: bare metal in QEMU ¶ A machine with no operating system under it: no libc, no POSIX, no firmware. The loader is a multiboot image that QEMU takes with -kernel ; it copies the kernel to 16 MiB, maps the same bytes at 0xFFFFFFFF80000000 - the higher half where the image is linked - builds the identity map of the first gigabyte and turns long mode on. make x86-build make x86-run # the window: VGA text and the PS/2 keyboard make x86-run-serial # the same machine in a terminal make x86-smoke # boot and check the transcript The processors come from the MADT of ACPI, and the boot prints how many the firmware describes and how many it runs: -smp 2 gives 2 cpu(s) reported by the firmware, 1 in use , because the APs wait for the trampoline of ADR 0012 that is not written yet. make x86-smp-build builds the portable kernel with KERNEL_SMP=ON . What works: the VGA text console and COM1 out of one k_port_write() , the PS/2 keyboard, the PIT, the context switch, the scheduler, paging and ring 3, NX/W^X (the text of the kernel and of a program is read-only code, every data page and stack is NX, and the boot audits the tables), the kernel in the higher half at 0xFFFFFFFF80000000 (ADR 0007), execve with MOX1 images, fork() with copy on write, MicroFS on the first partition of an ATA disk (or on 512 KB of RAM without one), the modes and the owners, and the network: a virtio-net card, ARP, ICMP, UDP, a client and a server of TCP and a resolver with a cache ( make x86-net-smoke ). It is the machine of programs.md and the proof that the kernel is portable. What does not: the second processor (the list is read, the AP bring-up is the blocker of ADR 0012, "The pilot of 1.x"), the key-value store (no /etc to persist), a second disk, DMA, SMAP/SMEP (a documented decision, ADR 0007), and the parts of the network that wait for a real link: DHCP, IPv6 and a congestion window. The details are in docs/ports/x86_64/README.md . host: the tests and the simulator ¶ A Linux process: threads instead of a scheduler substrate, pthread mutexes instead of a spinlock, files and sockets instead of a flash and a radio. It is the development loop and the machine of make test . make test # the unit tests, plus the null probe make sim # the whole system on a volume in a file make smoke # the same, driven by a script What works: everything portable, with the drivers stubbed and the console rendered into a file or nowhere. What it cannot do: run a program, and reproduce preemption - the critical section is a recursive pthread mutex, so a race is invisible unless the race detector looks for it ( make test-tsan ). The cores are a setting of the run: MICRO_OS_CPUS=2 tells the kernel it has two, and a task is then in the queue of one of them ( make test-smp , make test-tsan and make soak-host do it). Every task is already a pthread, so a "core" is a run queue and an identity of the task, not a worker thread. The details are in docs/ports/host/README.md . null: the port that is not a machine ¶ ports/port_null answers "there is no such thing" to every call: no console, no flash, no store, no sockets, no tasks. It is never run for a purpose. It exists for one check: microos_null_probe links the kernel and every portable component against it, so a symbol that portable code takes from a machine by accident stops the build on a laptop. It is compiled by the host build and run by ctest , and it is the compiled form of ADR 0004. It cannot catch a libc call - the probe is linked with the libc of the host - but it catches a leak of the port itself, which is the part that has to be complete. The details are in docs/ports/null/README.md . docs.text: Programs ¶ A program in Micro OS is a file , not a function of the kernel: execve reads the file through the VFS, the kernel checks it against a format of its own, and the port places it in memory and enters it. The decisions are in ADR 0005 (the format and the rights), ADR 0006 (the entry), ADR 0007 (the address space and ring 3) and ADR 0016 (the environment, the library and the programs of /bin ); the report of the phase is docs/phases/phase7.md . Two machines of the tree can run a program today: Machine k_port_exec_supported() k_port_exec_arch() What execve answers x86-64 in QEMU true 0 (x86-64) it runs the image in ring 3 ESP32 board true 1 (Xtensa) it runs the image in the kernel's address space (no protection) host simulator false 0 on x86-64, -1 elsewhere ENOSYS for its own machine, ENOEXEC for another, ENOSYS on a host of a machine the format does not know null port false -1 ENOSYS A port that cannot enter a program still names the machine it is, because the machine is a fact about the processor and the loader is a separate promise. The arch of the header is compared with k_port_exec_arch() before the port is asked anything: an image of another machine is ENOEXEC , and no byte of it is entered - the board checks this against a hand-made x86-64 image at every boot. In the simulator the shell still has exec ; it looks for the file, checks the execute bit, and then reports why the program did not run. That is the contract working, not a missing build. The format: MOX1, version 2 ¶ An executable is a flat image: a header of 32 bytes, then the code, then the initialised data. The bss is not in the file; the port clears it. The layout is in components/kernel/include/kernel/exec.h : Offset Field Meaning 0 magic the bytes M , O , X , 1 4 version 2 8 flags 0; a flag the kernel does not know is a refusal 12 entry the offset of the first instruction, from the start of the image 16 text_size the bytes of code 20 data_size the bytes of initialised data 24 bss_size the bytes to clear, at most 1 MiB 28 arch the machine of the bytes: 0 x86-64, 1 Xtensa 32 the text, then the data Version 2 is version 1 with the machine in the last field, which version 1 kept reserved and zero. The bytes of one machine are not the bytes of another, so an image says which machine it is for, and a reader that does not know a version refuses it instead of guessing at the meaning of the bytes. This kernel reads version 2 and refuses version 1 (and a later generation) with a sentence in the kernel log that names the version it reads; the call answers EINVAL . The parser ( components/kernel/src/exec.c ) checks the image against itself and nothing else: the magic and the version, an arch that is one of the two machines of the format, the sizes against the file, a text that is not empty, an entry inside the text, sizes that are multiples of four, a known flag, and a bss under a megabyte. Whether the image fits the window of the machine, and whether it is the right machine at all, is between the caller of k_exec_run and the port, asked later. tools/mkprog.sh turns a linked object into an image: tools/mkprog.sh [ --base 0x02000000 ] [ --data-base 0x3FFCE000 ] \ [ --arch x86-64 | xtensa ] hello.elf hello.mox hello_main The image is not relocated: the code and the data have to be linked for the address the port names, and --base makes the script refuse an image linked for another window. --arch writes the machine into offset 28 and defaults to x86-64 ; a name the format does not know is refused before an image is written. --data-base is for a port whose data is a window of its own (the board): the data no longer follows the text, so the script checks its address against that number instead of the contiguous rule and also checks where the bss will be cleared. The x86-64 port builds its sixteen images this way: the object is compiled for the window, linked with programs/program.ld , turned into a .mox by the script ( --base 0x02000000 --arch x86-64 ), and written into the MicroFS volume of the disk by make x86-disk (see below). The kernel carries no copy of a program. The board builds hello and cat with --arch xtensa --base 0x4009E000 --data-base 0x3FFCE000 and the toolchain of ESP-IDF (ADR 0018). The programs on the disk ¶ A program is a file of a volume, and the volume is a property of the disk of the machine. The gate opens for ring 3. The processor takes RSP0 from the TSS on the way in, so the handler runs on a kernel stack of the program, not on a stack the program could have pointed anywhere; the handler puts the kernel's thread pointer back, turns the interrupts on, calls ksys_call() and returns with iretq . The port notices the exit, unwinds to the call that entered it and reports the status (0..255). A program that faults is printed as the program faulted: vector N at 0x... , taken down, and its status is 255; the shell that ran it is alive and answers the next command. Both vectors are copied at the edge of the call: at most eight words and 512 bytes each, and a bad one is EFAULT or E2BIG before the file is read. exec /bin/cat /etc/setting passes no environment, and the kernel fills in the one of the system. The library of a program ¶ components/libc/user/ is the library a program is linked against; it is not the library of the kernel, which calls ksys_* and has no address in ring 3: File What it has include/ulibc.h the prototypes and the numbers of the calls, from kernel/ksys.h src/start.c _start : main(argc, argv, envp) , then exit ; on the board also the door, as the first argument src/syscall.c int $0x80 on x86-64 and the door of the port on the board; open , close , read , write , lseek , readdir , stat , mkdir , unlink , getcwd , getpid , uptime , execve , exit src/stdio.c printf and puts over a buffer of 128 bytes and write(1, ...) src/string.c strlen , strcmp , strncmp , strstr , memcpy , memset #include "ulibc.h" int main ( int argc , char * const argv [], char * const envp []) { int fd = open ( argv [ 1 ], ULIBC_O_RDONLY ); if ( fd < 0 ) { printf ( "cat: %s: error %d \n " , argv [ 1 ], - fd ); return ULIBC_EXIT_FAILURE ; } /* ... read and write ... */ close ( fd ); return ULIBC_EXIT_SUCCESS ; } The functions return the result of the call, so a negative number is -errno : the library has no errno of its own. There is no dynamic linker: each image carries its copy of the library. The address space and fork ¶ A program is a task of the scheduler with page tables of its own: the window is 16 MiB at 32 MiB ( 0x02000000 - 0x03000000 ), mapped onto a physical arena at 64 MiB; the kernel reaches the bytes through its identity map, the program through its own pages; the stack is 64 KiB at the top of the window, with an unmapped guard page below it; the null page is not mapped, so a write to address zero is a fault and not a silent success; the kernel is supervisor-only and out of the reach of ring 3; the program runs with cpl 3 and calls the kernel only through the gate. The kernel image itself is in the higher half ( 0xFFFFFFFF80000000 ), and a program's space names that map as it is, without the user bit; fork() copies the page tables, points both copies at the same frames read-only, and the first write of either side faults, copies the 4 KiB page and takes the write bit back. The child returns 0, the parent returns the pid, and waitpid() sees the status. On a machine without an MMU the same call is a placeholder: the child shares the memory of the parent and re-enters the program, and the port says so. There is no fork() with an address space of its own on the board, and no plan to pretend otherwise. What a program cannot do ¶ No ELF and no dynamic linker. The format is MOX1 , everything is statically linked, and there are no shared objects. No program of the board yet. The header knows the machine (ADR 0018) and mkprog.sh writes it, but the loader of the ESP32 port is not written: an Xtensa image on the board is still ENOSYS , and only x86-64 enters a program. The format is ready for the second machine; the port is not. No libc of the host. A program has the calls of the ABI, the library of components/libc/user and nothing else. The library is not a standard C library: no allocation, no files of a stream, no errno , no floating point (the programs are built with -mgeneral-regs-only ), and the formatter has no precision and no * width. No inherited descriptors. A program is a task with a table of four descriptors of its own, and the shell does not pass its own table to it. cat , wc , head and grep read descriptor 0 when they are given no file (or - ), but a fresh table has no descriptor 0: the read answers EBADF until a redirection or an inherited table opens it. The descriptors 1 and 2 are the console; pipe , dup2 and the inheritance are a debt of the milestone after this one. No mmap and no brk . A program cannot ask for a range of its own, and the library has no malloc . No shell export . The environment of every program is the four words of the kernel; a program that wants its own passes one to execve . No protection by SMAP yet. The edge checks the page tables of the caller and then reads the same pages in ring 0; the hardware half of the rule waits for the flags of the processor (SMEP) and the STAC / CLAC window of the copy (SMAP). The higher half is there. The open rows are in docs/debts.md ; the plan is docs/roadmap.md , K4 and K5. Back to the wiki index

docs.text: A program in Micro OS is a file , not a function of the kernel: execve reads the file through the VFS, the kernel checks it against a format of its own, and the port places it in memory and enters it. The decisions are in ADR 0005 (the format and the rights), ADR 0006 (the entry), ADR 0007 (the address space and ring 3) and ADR 0016 (the environment, the library and the programs of /bin ); the report of the phase is docs/phases/phase7.md . Two machines of the tree can run a program today: Machine k_port_exec_supported() k_port_exec_arch() What execve answers x86-64 in QEMU true 0 (x86-64) it runs the image in ring 3 ESP32 board true 1 (Xtensa) it runs the image in the kernel's address space (no protection) host simulator false 0 on x86-64, -1 elsewhere ENOSYS for its own machine, ENOEXEC for another, ENOSYS on a host of a machine the format does not know null port false -1 ENOSYS A port that cannot enter a program still names the machine it is, because the machine is a fact about the processor and the loader is a separate promise. The arch of the header is compared with k_port_exec_arch() before the port is asked anything: an image of another machine is ENOEXEC , and no byte of it is entered - the board checks this against a hand-made x86-64 image at every boot. In the simulator the shell still has exec ; it looks for the file, checks the execute bit, and then reports why the program did not run. That is the contract working, not a missing build.

docs.text: An executable is a flat image: a header of 32 bytes, then the code, then the initialised data. The bss is not in the file; the port clears it. The layout is in components/kernel/include/kernel/exec.h : Offset Field Meaning 0 magic the bytes M , O , X , 1 4 version 2 8 flags 0; a flag the kernel does not know is a refusal 12 entry the offset of the first instruction, from the start of the image 16 text_size the bytes of code 20 data_size the bytes of initialised data 24 bss_size the bytes to clear, at most 1 MiB 28 arch the machine of the bytes: 0 x86-64, 1 Xtensa 32 the text, then the data Version 2 is version 1 with the machine in the last field, which version 1 kept reserved and zero. The bytes of one machine are not the bytes of another, so an image says which machine it is for, and a reader that does not know a version refuses it instead of guessing at the meaning of the bytes. This kernel reads version 2 and refuses version 1 (and a later generation) with a sentence in the kernel log that names the version it reads; the call answers EINVAL . The parser ( components/kernel/src/exec.c ) checks the image against itself and nothing else: the magic and the version, an arch that is one of the two machines of the format, the sizes against the file, a text that is not empty, an entry inside the text, sizes that are multiples of four, a known flag, and a bss under a megabyte. docs.text: The port enters an image with the arguments of a C function in the registers ( ADR 0016 ): Register Argument rdi argc , the number of the words of argv rsi argv , the vector of the arguments, ended by NULL rdx envp , the vector of NAME=VALUE words, ended by NULL The stack is aligned as after a call and its top word is zero, so the C entry is main(argc, argv, envp) ; a program that returns instead of calling exit faults on address zero. The board has one argument in front of the three - the door of the port - and passes the four in a2 .. a5 of the windowed ABI; the _start of components/libc/user hides the difference from main . envp is never NULL: a program started without an environment of its own sees the four words of the system - PATH=/bin , HOME=/ , USER=root , PWD=/ - because the shell has no export yet. execve(path, argv, envp) is number 25, and the environment is its third argument, as in POSIX. Both vectors are copied at the edge of the call: at most eight words and 512 bytes each, and a bad one is EFAULT or E2BIG before the file is read. exec /bin/cat /etc/setting passes no environment, and the kernel fills in the one of the system.
