docs.text: A program is a task of the scheduler with page tables of its own: the window is 16 MiB at 32 MiB ( 0x02000000 - 0x03000000 ), mapped onto a physical arena at 64 MiB; the kernel reaches the bytes through its identity map, the program through its own pages; the stack is 64 KiB at the top of the window, with an unmapped guard page below it; the null page is not mapped, so a write to address zero is a fault and not a silent success; the kernel is supervisor-only and out of the reach of ring 3; the program runs with cpl 3 and calls the kernel only through the gate. The kernel image itself is in the higher half ( 0xFFFFFFFF80000000 ), and a program's space names that map as it is, without the user bit; fork() copies the page tables, points both copies at the same frames read-only, and the first write of either side faults, copies the 4 KiB page and takes the write bit back. The child returns 0, the parent returns the pid, and waitpid() sees the status. On a machine without an MMU the same call is a placeholder: the child shares the memory of the parent and re-enters the program, and the port says so. There is no fork() with an address space of its own on the board, and no plan to pretend otherwise.
docs.title: The address space and fork

docs.text: No ELF and no dynamic linker. The format is MOX1 , everything is statically linked, and there are no shared objects. No program of the board yet. The header knows the machine (ADR 0018) and mkprog.sh writes it, but the loader of the ESP32 port is not written: an Xtensa image on the board is still ENOSYS , and only x86-64 enters a program. The format is ready for the second machine; the port is not. No libc of the host. A program has the calls of the ABI, the library of components/libc/user and nothing else. The library is not a standard C library: no allocation, no files of a stream, no errno , no floating point (the programs are built with -mgeneral-regs-only ), and the formatter has no precision and no * width. No inherited descriptors. A program is a task with a table of four descriptors of its own, and the shell does not pass its own table to it. cat , wc , head and grep read descriptor 0 when they are given no file (or - ), but a fresh table has no descriptor 0: the read answers EBADF until a redirection or an inherited table opens it. The descriptors 1 and 2 are the console; pipe , dup2 and the inheritance are a debt of the milestone after this one. No mmap and no brk . A program cannot ask for a range of its own, and the library has no malloc . No shell export . The environment of every program is the four words of the kernel; a program that wants its own passes one to execve . No protection by SMAP yet. The edge checks the page tables of the caller and then reads the same pages in ring 0; the hardware half of the rule waits for the flags of the processor (SMEP) and the STAC / CLAC window of the copy (SMAP). The higher half is there. The open rows are in docs/debts.md ; the plan is docs/roadmap.md , K4 and K5. Back to the wiki index

docs.text: The 1.0 release ¶ This is the page of the first major release of Micro OS. It says what 1.0.0 is, what it promises, what it deliberately does not, and how a machine is updated from a 0.x release. The checklist behind it is the gate of 1.0 , and the decisions are ADR 0011 (versioning and the gate) and ADR 0012 (the second core, after this release). This page is the record of 1.0. The board changed with 1.1.0 : two application slots, an update over USB with a rollback and the programs in the progs partition (ADR 0022). The current layout and the one-time move of a board of 1.0 are in the notes of 1.1 . What 1.0 is ¶ Micro OS is a small operating system of its own: a portable C11 kernel, a syscall ABI of its own, MicroFS and FAT and an ext2 reader, a shell, and the same sources on two machines - the M5Stack StickC Plus2 (ESP32) and bare metal x86-64 in QEMU - with the host substrate (a Linux process) that runs the tests and the simulator, not a machine of its own. 1.0.0 is the point where the contracts stop moving: the system calls keep their numbers and their meaning, and a program built for 1.0.0 runs on every 1.x (the table is recorded in the tree and a test compares the record with the kernel on every build); the format of a program (MOX1 version 2) is frozen, with the machine of the image in its header; the format of a MicroFS volume is frozen; a volume of an older release mounts, and the release notes say what it cannot show (the times of a version 1 record are zero, which means "unknown"); the contract of a port is version 1.8 and every port implements it. What it promises ¶ A correct single-core kernel. The scheduler, the allocator, the VFS, the console and the block layer are safe with one core running the kernel, on both machines (and in the host substrate). The second core of the board is a project of 1.x, and this release does not pretend otherwise (ADR 0012). A program cannot reach the kernel on x86-64. Ring 3, page tables of its own, NX and W^X, copy_from_user and EFAULT at the edge of every call; a fault ends the program, not the shell. The board runs a program too , without an MMU: a .mox of Xtensa code, entered as a task with a door to the same system calls. There is no protection there, and the documentation says so in those words: a bad pointer or a fault in the program takes the board down. A filesystem that survives a power cut in the way the release notes describe: MicroFS has a check and a repair ( fsck -y ), FAT is written and repaired, ext2 is read. One system of processes : fork with copy on write on x86-64, execve with an environment, pipes and dup2 , four signals, a shell with pipelines and redirections, and ten real programs built against the library of a program. A network on both machines : an HTTP client, a page of the state, NTP, MQTT and telnet on the board; its own IPv4/TCP, a server half and a DNS cache on x86-64. No TLS: 1.0 is a LAN system, and that is the sentence of the readme and the release notes. The signature of an image ¶ The x86-64 machine boots a kernel only if its trailer says who signed it (ADR 0020). The image is the kernel and 120 bytes after it: the magic, the size, the SHA-256 of the bytes and an Ed25519 signature of those fields. The public key is compiled into the loader, so the image cannot bring a key of its own; the private key is not in this tree, and a release sets it with MICROOS_SIGN_KEY . The loader checks the trailer before it copies a byte of the kernel and before it turns the long mode on. A changed byte, a missing trailer and a signature of another key each print Micro OS: the image is refused: <reason> and halt; make x86-smoke proves all three, and the normal boot prints Micro OS: image signature ok (sha-256, ed25519) . tools/microos_sign sign and verify are the tools; make bundle signs the application of the board and leaves the .sig files and checksums.txt beside it. The check is a setting, not a wall. On x86-64 the CMake option MICRO_OS_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE is on by default; with it off the loader still verifies the image, prints Micro OS: unsigned or damaged image: not guaranteed and loads it. make x86-open-build builds that policy and make x86-smoke boots an unsigned and a damaged kernel on it. The board has the same setting in its Kconfig ( MICRO_OS_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE , on by default). At the beginning of app_main , before MicroFS and the shell, the firmware reads the factory partition: the ESP header says how long the image is, esp_app_desc_t says which version it is, and the trailer in the last 4 KiB of the partition carries the SHA-256 and the Ed25519 signature. The public key is compiled into the firmware and the flash layout does not change; tools/bundle.sh writes micro_os.bin.sig and flash.sh puts it at 0x20F000 . With the requirement on, a missing or wrong trailer stops the boot with boot: the image is refused: <reason> ; with it off, the console carries boot: unsigned or damaged image: not guaranteed and the board continues. tools/device-test.sh proves the signed image, the warning ( DEVICE_POLICY=unsigned ) and the stop ( DEVICE_POLICY=require-unsigned ). What "signed" does not mean on the board. The ROM and the ESP-IDF bootloader have already copied and entered the application when the check runs, so the first instructions of a damaged image execute before the sentence; it is an electronic check of the boot, not secure boot. A signature in the boot chain itself means secure boot v2, which burns eFuses, or a custom bootloader that does not fit the 28 KB bootloader partition. Neither is in 1.0. The check cannot stop a local attacker who can replace the firmware or the checker, and the signature does not hide the image. The anti-rollback is a second setting, MICRO_OS_ANTIROLLBACK , off by default. When it is on, the board keeps the newest version it has seen in the NVS and refuses a lower one (or prints a warning when the flag is off). It is not the eFuse counter of secure boot: a person who can flash the board can erase the NVS. x86-64 has no store that survives a reset, so a rollback there is allowed and there is no flag. Section 7 of the checklist is closed with the limits above written beside it. The session of 600 seconds ¶ No 1.0.0 is cut before one session of one boot runs 600 seconds under a mixed load without a bug : x86-64 with a disk and a network, a shell that runs programs, pipelines and redirections, fork , signals, files, ENOSPC and a repair, timers, and the host port under TSan at the same time. The board holds the same 600 seconds with programs, telnet, the network and the display. A panic, a hang, a reboot, a lost wakeup, a leak or a command that should pass and does not fails the session; a cosmetic line of the fourth level may stay. The campaign of 1.0 is in the wiki of the tests , and the tools are make soak , make soak-host , make board-soak , make fuzz-long and make disk-stress . What 1.0 does not have ¶ The release notes of 1.0.0 say the same list, so a person does not have to read the roadmap to learn it: the second core : the kernel is correct on one core; SMP is 1.x (ADR 0012); a safe update with a rollback : a device is updated over USB with a backup of its volume; the update path is the first block after 1.0.0 (ADR 0011, updated). The MICRO_OS_ANTIROLLBACK setting of the board refuses an old image, but it is not an update path and it does not put the old image back; TLS and IPv6 : 1.0 is a LAN system, without a certificate or a cloud account; a writable ext2 and a journal under FAT : ext2 is read, FAT is written without a log; more than one user : one uid, and the owner of a file is stored and checked but there is no a second party; an ARM port with an MMU : the first feature after the release; a progs partition of the board : the images of the board travel in the firmware and are written to /bin at the boot; a partition mapped as instructions is the next step (ADR 0018). Getting it ¶ The image for the board and the bundle of x86-64 are on the releases page of the repository. The board is written at 0x0 with flash.sh ; the machine of x86-64 is a loader and a flat kernel for QEMU, which boots from the disk image the build writes. The wiki of a version is at the root of this site for the latest stable, and under /dev/ for the development line. Upgrading from 0.x ¶ A volume of MicroFS, a /etc and a set of programs of a 0.x release are described in the migration guide : a version 1 record mounts and reports no time; /etc and /etc/fstab keep their files; the programs of /bin are files of the disk image, and an image built for 1.0 says its machine in the header (MOX1 version 2). The migration is tested on the release candidate, and a volume that cannot be read is named by fsck instead of being reformatted. The process behind the number ¶ The gate is a document, not a feeling: every line of docs/releases/1.0.md is [x] only when the code, the test and the run on the machine agree. A release candidate is cut when the gate holds, only fixes are allowed after it, and 1.0.0 follows at least two candidates without a change of an ABI, a format or a default. The four weeks on the board that the rule first asked for were waived by the owner: the session of 600 seconds of a candidate is the evidence, and it is what makes the number mean something.

docs.text: The 1.1 release ¶ 1.1.0 is the release of the board's last major changes. The ESP32 gets the settings of /etc , the programs in a partition of their own and an update with a rollback; the kernel gets the first phase of many cores. After this release the board is a compatibility port (ADR 0018): it keeps building and passing its test, and it receives only the changes that are cheap on this machine. The checklist is the notes of 1.1 ; the decisions are ADR 0021 (the settings), ADR 0022 (the layout) and ADR 0012 (many cores). A machine is set from the console ¶ The screen, the font and the console are files of /etc - display , font and console - in key=value lines, and the boot applies them before the first frame: microos> config set display.rotation 90 display: rotation 90, invert 1, brightness 100, theme dark display.rotation=90 microos> config set font.scale 2 font: scale 2, columns 0, rows 0 (0 is the whole picture) font.scale=2 microos> config sync config: 0 file(s) restored, 4 saved config get , config set , config list and config sync are the commands; the NVS keeps a copy, so a format or a flash does not cost the settings. A broken value falls back to its default with a warning, an unknown key is kept, and a machine without the hardware says that it does not apply the file rather than pretending. The full table of keys is in settings.md . The layout of the flash changes once ¶ The 8 MB are divided into two application slots of 1.125 MiB, progs of 132 KiB and 5.56 MiB of MicroFS for the user (against 5.94 MiB of 1.0). /bin is the progs partition: ls /bin lists cat and hello , and no image of a program is embedded in the firmware. A board of 1.0 loses its volume once , because the volume moves to a new offset. Back the files up, then flash with --erase-volume (or run mkfs -y at the shell). The NVS - the WiFi credentials, the settings of /etc - is not touched by the flash. An update can go back ¶ tools/ota_usb.py writes a newer image into the slot that is not running and resets the board. The bootloader keeps the new slot in PENDING_VERIFY until the shell has proved the boot (the kernel, MicroFS, /bin , the self test, the doctor and the console); a boot that never gets there, or an image whose signature does not match, is marked invalid and the previous slot starts. An update writes only the inactive slot and otadata ; MicroFS and the NVS are untouched. The network is not an update path in this release. The first phase of many cores ¶ Behind KERNEL_SMP (off by default) the kernel has a struct k_cpu per core, a run queue per core and a scheduler that never runs a task on two cores. The host substrate runs two "cores" in make test-smp , make test-tsan and make soak-host , and x86-64 reads the processor list of the machine and boots with -smp 2 in the smoke. The application processors of x86-64 are not started yet; that is the next phase of ADR 0012. Upgrading from 1.0 ¶ The syscall ABI, MOX1 and the format of a MicroFS volume do not change: a program and a volume of 1.0 work. Only the partition of the board moves, once, and only for the ESP32; the x86-64 port and the host substrate need nothing but the new image.

docs.text: The screen ¶ A machine of Micro OS has a screen and a serial console, and the kernel writes the same line to both. What the screen is depends on the port: a 135x240 TFT on the board, the text mode of the VGA on x86-64, and a window of QEMU or a real monitor in front of both. The board: a framebuffer of 135x240 ¶ The panel is an ST7789v2 of 135 by 240 pixels. The console draws into a framebuffer of the kernel ( kernel/render.h ) and a task flushes it to the panel; the font is 5x7, and the settings of /etc scale it: microos> config set display.rotation 90 display: rotation 90, invert 1, brightness 100, theme dark microos> config set font.scale 2 font: scale 2, columns 0, rows 0 (0 is the whole picture) rotation , invert , theme and font.scale are the keys of the systems of settings.md . brightness is kept and reported, but the pin of the backlight has no duty cycle yet, so the panel does not dim. x86-64: the text mode today ¶ The port draws into the text mode the firmware leaves behind: 80 columns by 25 rows at 0xB8000 , two bytes a cell, sixteen colours, no font and no picture. It is enough for a console a person types into, and it is all the machine has in 1.1: microos> config set console.theme light console: theme light, invert 0 console.theme and console.invert repaint every cell of the VGA. There is no graphics mode: no font of its own, no line, no picture, no window that is not the whole screen. The framebuffer of 1.2 (K11) ¶ ADR 0023 chooses the next screen: a linear framebuffer through Bochs VBE in QEMU, 1280x800 and 16 bits per pixel in RGB565, which is the format the renderer of the kernel already speaks. The console becomes a grid of the 5x7 font scaled twice - about 128 columns by 57 rows - with the colours of /etc/console , and the text mode stays the fallback (improved once to 80x50 with the 8x8 font of the VGA). The smoke reads the picture with screendump instead of the text memory of the VGA, so a change of the picture is visible in a screenshot, not only in a log line. What a desktop would need ¶ The framebuffer is the first step, not a desktop. A desktop needs a picture a program can draw on (a 2D surface), a pointer (the PS/2 mouse of QEMU), and a compositor - windows, focus and the routing of the input. The compositor has to be a program of the system, not the kernel, like X or Wayland; x86-64 already has ring 3, page tables of a program, NX/W^X, fork , exec , signals and pipes, which is the base of a screen server and its clients. The board cannot have one: no MMU, 2 MB of PSRAM, 135x240. The ESP32 stays a terminal. A 3D driver of a real card is not promised. virtio-gpu 2D in QEMU is an option after the framebuffer; a physical machine's picture needs UEFI GOP, which is a loader of its own and a separate change. The serial console ¶ COM1 of x86-64, the UART of the board and the pipes of the host substrate carry the same bytes as the screen. The settings of a screen never hide the serial line: a machine whose picture did not come up still speaks there, and the smoke reads both.

docs.text: The settings of a machine ¶ A few settings of a machine are data of /etc , and the screen, the font and the console are the first of them: one file per system of parameters, with key=value lines and comments. A person edits them with cat , write and config ; the boot applies them before the first frame; and the store of the port keeps them across mkfs -y . The decision and its reasons are ADR 0021 . What a system is ¶ /etc/display , the file of the screen of a machine: # the screen rotation=90 invert=0 brightness=100 theme=dark # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line; an empty line is not a line, and the spaces around a key and around a value are not part of either. a key is [a-z0-9_.-] and at most 15 characters; a value is at most 31 printable characters and is never cut. a later line of the same key wins. The file is not rewritten by a read, so the earlier line stays for the person who edits it. a line without = or with a key that is not one is skipped and counted; the boot names the number of skipped lines once in the log. a value the system cannot read (a number where a word belongs, 400 where 100 is the ceiling) is the default of the key and a warning. The file is not rewritten: the text stays what the person typed. a key the system does not know is kept in the file and named once in the log: a newer release may know it, and this one must not delete it. a file holds at most 12 pairs and 127 characters, because it is one value of the store of the port. A longer file is refused and the defaults are used. The three systems of the tree: System File Keys Defaults display /etc/display rotation 0/90/180/270, invert 0/1, brightness 0–100, theme dark/light 0, 1, 100, dark font /etc/font scale 1/2, columns 0–99, rows 0–99 1, 0, 0 console /etc/console invert 0/1, theme dark/light 0, dark columns=0 and rows=0 mean the whole picture: the console cuts the dialogue by the room the panel has at the size of the font. A positive value is a cap, so a person can keep the dialogue narrow on a wide screen. The defaults are the behaviour of the machine before the files existed, so a volume that never had /etc/display boots exactly like a release that did not have this feature. What each machine honours ¶ Key Board (ESP32) x86-64 Host display.rotation the picture is turned, before the first frame kept, not applied kept, not applied display.invert INVON/INVOFF of the glass kept, not applied kept, not applied display.brightness kept and a warning: the backlight is one pin, with no duty cycle to dim it kept, not applied kept, not applied display.theme the colours of the dialogue kept, not applied kept, not applied font.scale 2 doubles the 5x7 font and the cells of the console kept, not applied kept, not applied font.columns , font.rows a cap on the dialogue kept, not applied kept, not applied console.theme , console.invert the colours of the dialogue the attribute of every cell of the VGA kept, not applied display.theme and console.theme are the same picture on the board and the console is read after the display, so /etc/console wins when the two disagree. On x86-64 the theme is the attribute of the text screen: light grey on black for dark , black on light grey for light , and invert swaps the two (the number the port logs is 7 or 112 ). The host has no screen of its own: the load names the systems it cannot apply and keeps the files. The commands ¶ config without a word still lists the keys of the store of the port and their values, and config sync still restores and saves the files of /etc . microos> config list display /etc/display (not applied here) font /etc/font (not applied here) console /etc/console microos> config get display.rotation display.rotation=0 microos> config set console.theme light console: theme light, invert 0, the attribute of the screen 112 console.theme=light microos> config get console.theme console.theme=light microos> config set display.invert 0 display.invert=0 (kept: this machine does not apply display) microos> config list display display.rotation=0 display.invert=0 display.brightness=100 display.theme=dark config get <system>.<key> : the value of the file, or the default of the system when the file does not have the key. An unknown system or key is a sentence with the names that exist, not a silence. config set <system>.<key> <value> (or config set <system> <key> <value> ): the line of the file is replaced or appended, the file is written whole and the system is applied at once. A key the system does not know is refused, so a typo does not reach the file. config list [system] : the systems and their files, or every key of one system with its value. config sync : restore the missing files from the store and save the ones of /etc . The boot does the same on every start. A machine that cannot honour the system writes the file, logs the reason and answers SETTINGS_KEPT ; the shell prints the value with the sentence that says it is kept. That is not an error: a card with a /etc/display of another machine is a card that boots. When it is applied, and by whom ¶ The applier belongs to the machine and is registered with its system: Machine Where the applier is board components/drivers/src/drv_display.c ( display , font , console ) x86-64 ports/port_x86_64/src/vga.c ( console ) host none: the load names the three systems and keeps the files The order is the boot of the machine. The board loads the systems in the init task, after the volume is mounted and the files are restored, and before the task of the shell starts the console of the panel: the display and the font are the state of the first frame. x86-64 loads them in kmain() after the filesystem is up, so the attribute of the screen is right before the first command. The simulator loads them in its init task, and a run with a screen file still has no applier: the console of the host is a serial port. A format, and the store ¶ The files are the settings of /etc like any other, so the store of the port keeps them: config sync (and the boot) saves the text of every file under its name, and a volume that was formatted again gets the files back. mkfs -y takes the volume and not the store. idf.py erase-flash takes both. The write of a config set is one write of the whole text and the VFS has no rename , so it is not atomic: a power cut in the middle leaves a short file, the next boot reads the lines that are there, and config sync brings back the text of the last sync. That trade is written down in ADR 0021 . What it does not do ¶ No dimming of the panel. The backlight of the board is a pin: on or off. brightness is kept for a panel that can and is reported once per boot. No screen on the host. A machine that cannot honour a system keeps the file and says so; nothing is silently dropped. No schema and no type system. The applier of the machine reads its own keys; the tree knows the names of the keys so that config set can refuse a typo, and nothing more. No settings of a program. A program has its own files, not /etc . No per-key write. A config set writes the whole file, and the nine other keys are copied as they are. The tests are tests/cases/test_settings.c on the host (the parser, the rewrite, the defaults, the appliers, set / get and a format through the store), the config commands of make x86-smoke , and the device test of the board ( config set display.rotation 90 , the log of the display, a reboot). docs.text: The shell ¶ Every boot ends at a prompt: MicroOS shell ready. Type 'help' for the list of commands. microos> The shell is components/kshell , part of the kernel: the same interpreter and the same commands on the board, in the simulator and on x86-64. A port or a driver adds commands of its own by registering them by name, which is why the list is not the same on every machine. The line ¶ The line is split on spaces and tabs; there are no quotes, no escapes and no globs. A line is at most 127 characters and at most 8 words per stage. Backspace erases, Ctrl+C throws the line away, and a line that did not fit is not executed (the shell says line too long, it was not executed ), because a cut line is a different command. While a program or a pipe runs, Ctrl+C is not a line: the shell reads it and sends SIGINT to the program or to every stage of the chain (see kernel-abi.md ). Because there are no quotes, a command that needs an empty argument accepts the two characters "" as the way to type it. path "" is the example. A name that is not registered answers <name>: command not found . A command that is given the wrong arguments answers with its own usage: line and does nothing. Pipes and redirections ¶ | joins two or more stages, and > , >> , < , 2> and 2>> send a descriptor of a stage to a file. The operators are words of their own, with a space around them, because the splitter has no quotes; they may stand before or after the arguments of a stage: microos> ls /etc | cat microos> echo one | cat | cat microos> cat /etc/setting > /tmp/f microos> cat /etc/setting >> /tmp/f microos> cat < /etc/setting microos> cat /etc/setting 2> /tmp/errors microos> /bin/cat /etc/setting | wc -l A stage that is a command of the shell ( ls , cat , echo , df , ...) runs in a task of its own and writes descriptor 1, so a redirect or a pipe carries its output exactly as it carries a program's. A name that is not a command is looked up in PATH and started with execve ; on x86-64 that program inherits the three descriptors of the stage, which is what makes echo one | /bin/cat and ls /bin | wc -l work. On the board and in the simulator there is no program to run, and only the commands of the shell can be stages. What the line does not do: no && , || , ; or & : they are refused by name, not run as arguments; no 2>&1 , no >& , no file-descriptor juggling beyond 0 , 1 and 2 ; no quotes, escapes, globs or variables: * is a word and not a pattern; no attached forms: a|b and >file are arguments; write a | b , > file ; at most three stages, because a boundary is a pipe and the shell task has four descriptors; no background job, no jobs , no fg or bg ; a command that changes the task of the shell ( cd , path ) cannot be a stage or carry a redirection: it is refused with a sentence instead of changing a copy nobody sees. The status of a line is the status of its last stage. A program that is the last stage answers 0 when it ran and 1 when it could not start; its own code is not handed back by execve yet. help ¶ microos> help command what it does mkfs format the volume: mkfs -y ... microos> help exec exec: run a program: exec <program> [args...] help with an argument prints the same text as <command> --help : the usage line, the summary and the notes. help --help explains help itself. Options and -h / --help ¶ Every command answers -h and --help without running: a usage: line, the summary from the table of the commands and the notes of the command. The flag has to be the first word of the line; a -h deeper in the arguments is a character the command sees. -- ends the options, so a name that starts with - can still be passed. A command that does not have a flag refuses it: ls -z prints ls: unknown option: -z and the usage line. df -h is the one GNU-shaped exception: -h asks for human sizes, so the help of df is df --help . The commands ¶ The core of the kernel, on every machine: Command What it does help [command] the list of commands, or the full help of one uname the name, the version, the architecture and the build id uptime the time since the boot, the ticks and the task count ps the tasks: pid, priority, state, name free the memory of the heap and of the PSRAM dmesg the log of the boot, from the ring buffer of the kernel echo <words> print the words sleep <milliseconds> wait, up to 60000 clear clear the screen (the escape sequence the panel and the VGA read) modules run the hardware doctor and print its report abi the table of the system calls ulimit [-m bytes \| -c ms \| -n fds] the limits of the shell, or lower one of them memtest [kilobytes] measure the memory and its speed mfetch [color] the system report with a logo reboot restart the machine The files, on every machine: Command What it does pwd , cd <dir> the current directory ls [-la] [path] the names of a directory, one per line; -l adds the mode, the owner, the size and the date, -a puts . and .. first tree [-ad] [path] the levels below a path, with `-- branches; -d keeps the directories only cat [-n] [file] the content of a file, or of the standard input; -n numbers the lines write <file> <text> create or replace a file with one line (at most 127 bytes) mkdir <dir> , rm [-r] <file> a directory, a file; a directory needs -r df [-h] [path] the free blocks and inodes; -h in KB/MB mount the mounted filesystems fsck [fat <point\|device> [-y]] check a volume: MicroFS, or the FAT volume at a point or on a device; -y repairs the FAT volume stat <path> the type, the mode, the owner and the size chmod <mode> <path> , chown <uid> <path> the mode (octal) and the owner (0..32767) path [directories] show or set PATH exec <program> [args...] run a program, by a path or found in PATH kill [-signal] <pid> send INT , TERM , CHLD or PIPE to a task; TERM by default The services, where the port registers them: Command What it does Where config , config sync list the store of /etc , restore and save it board, simulator mkfs -y format the volume (erases everything) board, simulator http get <url> one HTTP request; prints the status and the body board ntp [server] set the clock from NTP (UTC), default pool.ntp.org board httpd [port\|off] the page of the state over HTTP, default port 80 board mqtt <host> <port> <topic> <message> publish one message at QoS 0 board telnet [on\|off] the shell on port 23 board date , date set <YYYY-MM-DD> <HH:MM:SS> the RTC, or the clock of the host board, simulator battery , beep [frequency] [ms] , led on\|off\|heart\|dance the power cell, the buzzer, the LED board, simulator (stubs) input [seconds] watch the buttons board, simulator (stubs) wifi [status\|scan\|connect <ssid> [key]\|join\|disconnect\|forget] the WiFi station board, simulator (stub) display [<x> <y>] \| rotate <0\|90\|180\|270> \| invert [on\|off] \| draw [seconds] the panel board i2c scan the I2C bus board mic the level of the microphone board rtc alarm [HH:MM\|+<seconds>\|day <1-31> HH:MM\|clear] the alarm of the BM8563 and its flag board power [sleep <seconds>\|off] deep sleep with the timer or button C, or power off board factory reset -y erase MicroFS and the NVS, then restart; without -y it only explains board The simulator has no network and no drivers: http , ntp , httpd , mqtt and telnet are not registered there at all, and the driver commands of the board are stubs that answer something sensible. The x86-64 port registers only the core and the files: no config , no mkfs , no date , no network. This is the port boundary doing its job, not a bug; ports.md has the whole matrix. PATH and exec ¶ PATH starts at /bin:/usr/bin and belongs to the shell: it is not a file of /etc , and a program does not inherit it yet. microos> path /bin:/usr/bin microos> path /bin microos> path "" A name with a slash is a path and is used as it is. A name without one is looked up in PATH , and the first regular file with an execute bit wins; a file without the bit is passed over, as in Linux. A search that found nothing says where it looked: microos> exec hello exec: hello: not found in /bin:/usr/bin On the board and in the simulator there is no program to run: a fresh volume has no /bin , and execve answers ENOSYS even for a file that is there. The x86-64 port has /bin in the MicroFS volume of its disk image ( make x86-disk ): hello , crash , fork , badptr , signals , cat , echo , ls , wc , head , grep , mkdir , rm , pwd and spawn are files with the mode 0755, and the boot and the shell run them as programs of ring 3. The library programs inherit the descriptors of the shell, so a pipeline can end in one of them. programs.md explains what a program is. kill , Ctrl+C and no job control ¶ There is no job control: no & , no fg , no bg , no groups of processes and no SIGSTOP . A program runs in the foreground until it ends, and the shell waits for it. docs.text: Every boot ends at a prompt: MicroOS shell ready. Type 'help' for the list of commands. microos> The shell is components/kshell , part of the kernel: the same interpreter and the same commands on the board, in the simulator and on x86-64. A port or a driver adds commands of its own by registering them by name, which is why the list is not the same on every machine.

docs.text: The line is split on spaces and tabs; there are no quotes, no escapes and no globs. A line is at most 127 characters and at most 8 words per stage. Backspace erases, Ctrl+C throws the line away, and a line that did not fit is not executed (the shell says line too long, it was not executed ), because a cut line is a different command. While a program or a pipe runs, Ctrl+C is not a line: the shell reads it and sends SIGINT to the program or to every stage of the chain (see kernel-abi.md ). Because there are no quotes, a command that needs an empty argument accepts the two characters "" as the way to type it. path "" is the example. A name that is not registered answers <name>: command not found . A command that is given the wrong arguments answers with its own usage: line and does nothing.
docs.title: The line

docs.text: | joins two or more stages, and > , >> , < , 2> and 2>> send a descriptor of a stage to a file. The operators are words of their own, with a space around them, because the splitter has no quotes; they may stand before or after the arguments of a stage: microos> ls /etc | cat microos> echo one | cat | cat microos> cat /etc/setting > /tmp/f microos> cat /etc/setting >> /tmp/f microos> cat < /etc/setting microos> cat /etc/setting 2> /tmp/errors microos> /bin/cat /etc/setting | wc -l A stage that is a command of the shell ( ls , cat , echo , df , ...) runs in a task of its own and writes descriptor 1, so a redirect or a pipe carries its output exactly as it carries a program's. A name that is not a command is looked up in PATH and started with execve ; on x86-64 that program inherits the three descriptors of the stage, which is what makes echo one | /bin/cat and ls /bin | wc -l work. On the board and in the simulator there is no program to run, and only the commands of the shell can be stages. What the line does not do: no && , || , ; or & : they are refused by name, not run as arguments; no 2>&1 , no >& , no file-descriptor juggling beyond 0 , 1 and 2 ; no quotes, escapes, globs or variables: * is a word and not a pattern; no attached forms: a|b and >file are arguments; write a | b , > file ; at most three stages, because a boundary is a pipe and the shell task has four descriptors; no background job, no jobs , no fg or bg ; a command that changes the task of the shell ( cd , path ) cannot be a stage or carry a redirection: it is refused with a sentence instead of changing a copy nobody sees. The status of a line is the status of its last stage. A program that is the last stage answers 0 when it ran and 1 when it could not start; its own code is not handed back by execve yet.

docs.text: Testing ¶ The checks are layered by what they can see. A unit test sees one piece of the kernel; the simulator sees the whole portable system as a process; the x86-64 smoke test sees a bare machine and a processor; the device test sees the board and the chips on it. None of them replaces another. The commands ¶ Command What it proves Needs make test the host build, the unit tests, the null probe gcc , cmake , ninja make test-asan the same tests with the sanitizers the same make test-tsan the same tests under the race detector, on two cores the same make test-smp the tests of the kernel of two cores ( KERNEL_SMP ) the same make test-minimal the host tests with the optional features off the same make smoke the simulator boots and the shell answers the host build make coverage the lines of components/kernel and the threshold gcc , gcov , Python make reproducible two runs of the disk image are the same bytes gcc , cmake , ninja make x86-build the x86-64 kernel and loader compile gcc , cmake , ninja make x86-smp-build the same kernel with KERNEL_SMP=ON (ADR 0012) gcc , cmake , ninja make x86-smoke the kernel boots, runs /bin/hello , the shell answers qemu-system-x86_64 make x86-vga-smoke the VGA screen and the PS/2 keyboard, no display qemu-system-x86_64 make x86-disk-smoke a file written by one boot is read by the next qemu-system-x86_64 make x86-net-smoke the network: ping, UDP, HTTP, httpd and DNS qemu-system-x86_64 make soak one boot of x86-64 for 600 s under the mixed load QEMU, the host build make soak-host the portable kernel on the host under TSan for 600 s, two cores GCC, TSan, valgrind make fuzz-long the fuzz of the ABI and the parsers, with a multiplier GCC, ASan make disk-stress a full volume, fsck -y and two boots (MicroFS, FAT) QEMU, dosfstools, mtools make board-soak the same session on the board, one boot ESP-IDF and a board make integrity the boundary, the bundle, the partitions, the hygiene clang-format make ci the list a contributor runs before a push the above, QEMU optional tools/device-test.sh build, flash and boot the board ESP-IDF and a board make test : the unit tests ¶ make test configures and builds build-host/ and runs ctest , which runs three tests: microos_tests - the unit tests, in tests/cases/ , on the framework of tests/framework/ktest.h . There is no external dependency; the tests run inside a real kernel task, so they exercise the task API as well. mkprog - tools/test_mkprog.py , the layout of the image that tools/mkprog.sh writes; it builds tiny objects with the compiler of the host and skips itself when Python is not found. null_probe - the kernel and every portable component linked against the null port. A symbol that portable code takes from a machine by accident is a link error here, on a laptop. The numeric corpus is tests/corpus/vectors.txt : 512 numbers with the boundary values (0, 1, 255, 65535, 2147483647 and so on) mixed in. A new numeric behaviour reuses it rather than inventing a second list. make test-asan and make test-tsan are the same tests in build-asan/ and build-tsan/ . The board has no debugger, so the host is the place where a wrong pointer or undefined behaviour has to be caught; TSan is the only thing that sees a race, because the host port cannot reproduce preemption. make test-minimal is the second configuration of the host build (ADR 0010): KERNEL_PSRAM , KERNEL_EXEC , the network components and the second filesystem are off, in build-minimal/ . It proves that the sources still build without them and runs the tests that do not need the feature - the cases of exec and of the network are guarded in the source, so the report still says how many checks the small build has. make smoke : the simulator ¶ make smoke runs tools/sim_smoke.py , which boots build-host/ports/port_host/microos_sim with a volume and a store of its own, types a list of commands and checks the transcript: the subsystems, MicroFS, /proc , /dev , the configuration of /etc , the shell and the network. It is the cheapest end-to-end test of the portable system, and it takes a couple of seconds. The simulator links components/net , so the same HTTP client, clock of NTP and page of the state the board runs over lwIP run there over the sockets of the process. The smoke test starts a small page of its own on the loopback and asks the guest for it with http get , so the path from the shell through the client to a real socket is exercised, not only the parser of a unit test. It does not open a port on the network of the machine: the page lives in the test process, on a port the kernel chose. make sim runs the same binary by hand, with /tmp/microos-sim.img and /tmp/microos-kv by default. python3 tools/sim_smoke.py --verbose shows every step. make reproducible : the same inputs, the same bytes ¶ The gate of 1.0 asks for an image that two runs build to the same bytes. Three things used to make that fail: the records of MicroFS are stamped with mtime and ctime , and the filesystem took the moment from the clock of the process; kernel_build_id() is __DATE__ " " __TIME__ , which changes on every compile; an absolute path of the source tree reached the debug information and __FILE__ of a panic message. make exports SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH (0 by default, the convention of reproducible builds); make reproducible builds the disk image, keeps a copy, builds it again from nothing and compares the two with cmp , then prints their sha256 . The campaign runs on a release candidate and its report is attached to the candidate. One boot, 600 seconds: make soak ¶ make soak # 600 s, one boot of the x86-64 machine make soak SOAK_MINUTES = 1 # the smoke test of the tool itself The target builds build-x86-net (the port with the network and its disk) and a full volume ( tools/soak_image.py ), then tools/soak.py boots the machine once and types a cycle of commands until the clock says stop: the shell: uname , uptime , free , df , ulimit , ps , mount , tree , fsck , kill of a pid nobody has, sleep ; every program of /bin through exec : hello , cat , echo , ls , wc , grep , head , mkdir , rm , pwd , spawn , fork , signals , nx , badptr , crash ; pipelines and redirections: ls /bin | wc -l , cat < f | wc -l , echo x > f , echo y >> f , and a read of the file back; the filesystem: a directory, a program's rm -r , files written, appended and removed; once per boot the volume starts with no free block , one write is refused with ENOSPC , the filler leaves, fsck -y repairs and the volume is used again; signals: exec /bin/signals and Ctrl+C typed into the console while the program runs; the network: ping 10.0.2.2 , the HTTP client against a page of the process, the httpd page reached through hostfwd , and DNS when this host can resolve a name. The direct form has the same options: tools/soak.py --minutes 1 , --seconds , --seed , --keep-logs , --no-net , --hang-seconds . --iterations N is the other mode: N short boots, one cycle each, with the average boot reported. It is for the days before the higher half; the gate is the single 600-second session. A session fails on any of: a Panic , a Guru Meditation , a triple fault , Rebooting , a failed assertion or *** ERROR in the console; QEMU going away before the clock ends (a reset is the end of the boot); the console silent for --hang-seconds (30 by default), or a command that does not answer inside --timeout ; a command of the load whose answer lacks the word it must have; a heap that lost more than --mem-drift-kb (16 KB by default), a shell that holds memory at rest, a changed descriptor limit, or a task table that grew; a difference between the free / ulimit / ps / df samples before and after the load. NTP is skipped with a line of the report when the process cannot bind UDP 123: the kernel asks 10.0.2.2:123 , which QEMU maps to the loopback of the host, and a laptop has no privilege for the port. The transcript of a failed session is written to build-x86-net/soak-logs/ (and --keep-logs writes the one of a pass); the report prints the path. The host half: make soak-host ¶ make soak-host # TSan for 600 s and one valgrind run make soak-host HOST_SOAK_MINUTES = 1 tools/host_stress.c is the load: four tasks of the host port at once, each allocating and freeing blocks of kmm , making pipes, creating, rewriting and removing files, and forking a child that exits ( task_fork_shared ). The first boot finds a full volume ( ENOSPC ), removes the filler, repairs with fsck -y , writes, appends, makes and removes a directory, and leaves a file for the second boot. The second boot checks the volume, reads the file, and runs and removes again. The verdict is that the volume is either whole or made whole by the repair: fsck says the volume is consistent , or 0 problem(s) after the repair , and never a problem after it. The report prints the heap, the free blocks, the descriptors and the tasks before and after, and the drift the run allows. Reading a result and the levels of a bug ¶ A pass is the last line RESULT: PASS 600s (the x86 and host sessions), RESULT: PASS (N short iteration(s)) for --iterations , or RESULT: PASS 600s from the board. The report above it is the evidence: duration, boot, cycles, commands, memory/descriptors/tasks before and after, and the first failures with the line of the answer. Attach it to the candidate with the uname of the build, the command, the seed, the logs of build-*/soak-logs/ , and the lines network ... ntp ... dns ... that say which halves actually ran. The campaign classifies what it finds: L1 — a crash, a loss of data or a security hole. A panic, a reboot, a triple fault, a corrupted volume that fsck -y cannot repair, a file that disappears, a task that faults where the kernel should have answered EFAULT . Always a blocker. L2 — a feature is broken. A command of the load that must pass and does not, a fsck that leaves a problem, a fork or a signal with a wrong answer, a leak that grows with the load. Always a blocker. L3 — an edge or a rare race. A TSan warning, a window that needs a seed and many iterations, an ENOSPC path that leaves a surprise. A blocker for 1.0 unless it is recorded as a debt with its next step and its workaround; the g_last_error above is such a case. L4 — cosmetic. A line of output, a message of the log, a spelling. It changes no result and may stay at the release. The four levels are the same on every machine. A failure of a tool that has not been run (a skipped network or a missing mcopy ) is not a pass: the report says skip , and the release notes say which halves were skipped. Back to the wiki index

The campaign is the four tools below, on the two machines and the host substrate: unit soak fuzz stress host make test , make test-asan , make test-tsan make soak-host (TSan, 600 s) make fuzz-long valgrind, inside soak-host x86-64 make test (the same sources) make soak (one boot, 600 s) make fuzz-long make disk-stress board tools/device-test.sh tools/board_soak.sh (600 s) — fsck in the board session make ci does not include the campaign: ten minutes of QEMU and a board do not belong to a push. The campaign runs on a release candidate and its report is attached to the candidate.
docs.title: The campaign of 1.0

docs.text: make soak # 600 s, one boot of the x86-64 machine make soak SOAK_MINUTES = 1 # the smoke test of the tool itself The target builds build-x86-net (the port with the network and its disk) and a full volume ( tools/soak_image.py ), then tools/soak.py boots the machine once and types a cycle of commands until the clock says stop: the shell: uname , uptime , free , df , ulimit , ps , mount , tree , fsck , kill of a pid nobody has, sleep ; every program of /bin through exec : hello , cat , echo , ls , wc , grep , head , mkdir , rm , pwd , spawn , fork , signals , nx , badptr , crash ; pipelines and redirections: ls /bin | wc -l , cat < f | wc -l , echo x > f , echo y >> f , and a read of the file back; the filesystem: a directory, a program's rm -r , files written, appended and removed; once per boot the volume starts with no free block , one write is refused with ENOSPC , the filler leaves, fsck -y repairs and the volume is used again; signals: exec /bin/signals and Ctrl+C typed into the console while the program runs; the network: ping 10.0.2.2 , the HTTP client against a page of the process, the httpd page reached through hostfwd , and DNS when this host can resolve a name. The direct form has the same options: tools/soak.py --minutes 1 , --seconds , --seed , --keep-logs , --no-net , --hang-seconds . --iterations N is the other mode: N short boots, one cycle each, with the average boot reported. It is for the days before the higher half; the gate is the single 600-second session. A session fails on any of: a Panic , a Guru Meditation , a triple fault , Rebooting , a failed assertion or *** ERROR in the console; QEMU going away before the clock ends (a reset is the end of the boot); the console silent for --hang-seconds (30 by default), or a command that does not answer inside --timeout ; a command of the load whose answer lacks the word it must have; a heap that lost more than --mem-drift-kb (16 KB by default), a shell that holds memory at rest, a changed descriptor limit, or a task table that grew; a difference between the free / ulimit / ps / df samples before and after the load. The numbers are printed in the report. NTP is skipped with a line of the report when the process cannot bind UDP 123: the kernel asks 10.0.2.2:123 , which QEMU maps to the loopback of the host, and a laptop has no privilege for the port. That is a skip and not a pass; a runner with CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (or a network namespace) runs it. The transcript of a failed session is written to build-x86-net/soak-logs/ (and --keep-logs writes the one of a pass); the report prints the path.
docs.title: One boot, 600 seconds: make soak

docs.text: make soak-host # TSan for 600 s and one valgrind run make soak-host HOST_SOAK_MINUTES = 1 tools/host_stress.c is the load: four tasks of the host port at once, each allocating and freeing blocks of kmm , making pipes, creating, rewriting and removing files, and forking a child that exits ( task_fork_shared ). The version built in build-tsan is the one that matters: the host port stands in for the critical section with a mutex and cannot show preemption, so TSan is the only reader of a race here. The tool fails on a WARNING: ThreadSanitizer (and prints the location it names), on a stress that stops printing (a deadlock), on a run that ends before its time, on a block the allocator still holds, on a task left in the table, or on a definite leak of valgrind. One run of 5 seconds under valgrind is a part of the target; --skip-valgrind is for a machine without it. The first campaign of this tree named a race that the shorter tests never saw: g_last_error in components/kernel/src/vfs.c is written by every VFS call from the tasks' threads and is read by nobody. It is an open debt in docs/debts.md ; until it is closed, make soak-host fails, which is the correct answer of the tool.
docs.title: The host half: make soak-host

docs.text: make fuzz-long # 20x the iterations, seed 0 make fuzz-long FUZZ_ITERATIONS = 200 FUZZ_SEED = 7 The suite is the ordinary one in the sanitizer build; the campaign only moves two numbers of tests/cases/test_fuzz.c through the environment: KTEST_FUZZ_ITERATIONS multiplies the loops and KTEST_FUZZ_SEED changes the seed of the MOX1 and MicroFS streams. The binary still runs every case, so the ABI edge ( test_ksys ), FAT, ext2 and the network are exercised in the same run. A long run is repeatable: the same seed and the same multiplier give the same sequence on every machine.
docs.title: The fuzz: make fuzz-long

docs.text: tools/disk_stress.py boots the image twice. The first boot finds a full volume ( ENOSPC ), removes the filler, repairs with fsck -y , writes, appends, makes and removes a directory, and leaves a file for the second boot. The second boot checks the volume, reads the file, and runs and removes again. The verdict is that the volume is either whole or made whole by the repair: fsck says the volume is consistent , or 0 problem(s) after the repair , and never a problem after it. MicroFS is checked on build-x86 ; FAT is checked in a second partition of an image of build-x86-fat (the port with MICRO_OS_FS_FAT32=ON ), filled with mcopy and repaired with fsck fat -y . Those two halves need mkfs.vfat and mcopy ; when they are not installed the FAT half is reported as skipped, and --require-fat turns that skip into a failure for a runner that must have them.
docs.title: The disk: make disk-stress

docs.text: tools/board_soak.sh # build, flash, 600 s tools/board_soak.sh --minutes 1 # the tool itself tools/board_soak.sh --no-build --no-flash # the firmware already there The script does what tools/device-test.sh does (finds ESP-IDF, builds, flashes) and then tools/board_soak_session.py resets the board once and spends one boot with it: exec /bin/hello with arguments, cat of a file written by the shell, files appended and removed, mkdir / rm -r , the foreign image's exec format error , fsck , telnet on/off , wifi status , display rotate , mfetch , modules , sleep , abi , ps and ulimit . A panic, a Guru Meditation , a backtrace, a reboot, a silence or a descriptor/memory/volume/task drift beyond the small allowance fails it. The report prints the heap, the free blocks, the descriptors and the tasks before and after, and the drift the run allows.
docs.title: The board: tools/board_soak.sh

docs.text: A pass is the last line RESULT: PASS 600s (the x86 and host sessions), RESULT: PASS (N short iteration(s)) for --iterations , or RESULT: PASS 600s from the board. The report above it is the evidence: duration, boot, cycles, commands, memory/descriptors/tasks before and after, and the first failures with the line of the answer. Attach it to the candidate with the uname of the build, the command, the seed, the logs of build-*/soak-logs/ , and the lines network ... ntp ... dns ... that say which halves actually ran. The campaign classifies what it finds: L1 — a crash, a loss of data or a security hole. A panic, a reboot, a triple fault, a corrupted volume that fsck -y cannot repair, a file that disappears, a task that faults where the kernel should have answered EFAULT . Always a blocker. L2 — a feature is broken. A command of the load that must pass and does not, a fsck that leaves a problem, a fork or a signal with a wrong answer, a leak that grows with the load. Always a blocker. L3 — an edge or a rare race. A TSan warning, a window that needs a seed and many iterations, an ENOSPC path that leaves a surprise. A blocker for 1.0 unless it is recorded as a debt with its next step and its workaround; the g_last_error above is such a case. L4 — cosmetic. A line of output, a message of the log, a spelling. It changes no result and may stay at the release. The four levels are the same on every machine. A failure of a tool that has not been run (a skipped network or a missing mcopy ) is not a pass: the report says skip , and the release notes say which halves were skipped. Back to the wiki index

Network commands ¶ The network of 1.0 is the LAN : HTTP, MQTT and telnet are plain text, there is no TLS/HTTPS, no certificate store, no IPv6 and no raw sockets, and httpd and telnet take no password. Keep the machine on the network of its owner; SECURITY.md says what that means. httpd: the port 80 is not ours — the port is held, or the stack refused. Try httpd 8080 and check wifi status . httpd: already on port 80 — the server is on. httpd off , then httpd <port> . http: <url>: the connection failed — no route, no DNS, or the server is down. Check wifi status , try an address; there is no TLS. the URL is not one we speak — the scheme is not plain HTTP, or there is no host. Only http:// with a host is understood; there is no https:// . ntp: no answer from ... — UDP 123 is blocked, or the server is silent. Try ntp time.google.com . mqtt: no session with the broker — the broker is unreachable on that port. Check host and port; there is no TLS. mqtt: the broker refused the client — the broker said no. The client id is microos ; check its rules. mqtt: the message is longer than 256 byte(s) — the payload limit. Shorten it; a topic is 128 bytes at most. mqtt cannot reach a broker on 8883 — that is the TLS port, and 1.0 has no TLS. Use 1883 on the LAN, or terminate TLS on another machine. telnet connects but nothing happens — the door is off. telnet on ; the port is 23, no authentication. telnet answers anyone who connects — there is no password and no TLS. Keep it on the LAN and run telnet off when it is not needed.
